Classifying Market Regimes

What to measure, which regimes to name, where training labels come from, and what a causal classifier can learn

Abstract

Classifying the market regime usually means forecasting part of the future. The regimes worth building are defined by how much the market will move, which can be forecast. Regimes defined by which way it will move cannot be forecast, according to a century of US data.

A regime definition is a choice. Eight reasonable definitions of a bad market, from bear markets to recessions to volatile months ahead, agree only moderately over a century of US data. Most regime vocabularies divide five quantities into a few states: risk, the compensation for risk, drift, the economy, and co-movement. Many labels use future data. A day counts as part of a bear market because prices fell 20% afterward. From 1927 to 2025, leaving the market during bear markets known in hindsight would have raised the Sharpe ratio from 0.45 to 1.54. Leaving when the 20% rule actually confirmed each bear market gave 0.46. The confirmation came a median of 70 trading days after the peak.

Risk persists, so it can be forecast. A simple model ranked a day before a volatile month above a day before a calm month 88% of the time, and last month’s volatility alone did so 84% of the time. The same model forecast the sign of the next quarter’s return slightly worse than a coin flip. The VIX, credit spreads, the yield curve and the volatility term structure largely repeat what recent price variation already shows. In the worked example they added almost nothing to seven price-based features, and 19 more years of history were worth more than any extra feed. Each label source has a reach: how far into the future it looks. The reach sets how the training data must be split and how late any detection will be. Official recession dates arrive 7 to 15 months late on average.

Because regimes persist, the most recent known label is a strong baseline, and a model must beat it, not a coin flip. A small, regularized model usually matches a complex one, because there are only a few dozen crises to learn from. A quarter-century of daily data holds nine bear markets, so evaluate per episode, with error bars that reflect the small count. The chapter recommends defining the regime by the risk a decision depends on over the next few weeks, and never training on a label before it could have been known.

What this is. A practitioner who sets out to “detect the market regime” meets four questions that the phrase hides. Which definition of a regime should the study adopt? Which observable inputs carry information about it? If a model is to be trained, where do the training labels come from? And which model turns the inputs into a classification? This chapter answers them in that order (§2–§5). Its companion, Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models, treats a regime as a latent state and builds the hidden Markov model that infers it. This chapter treats a regime as a target: something a decision needs, defined explicitly, and estimated from data available at the time. Most of its length goes to the two questions the latent-state view leaves open: what to feed a classifier, and what to train it against.

How to read it. Part I (§1–§2) states the problem and surveys the regime definitions practitioners use. Part II (§3–§4) covers inputs and labels, the two sections a reader building a regime study will use most. Part III (§5–§8) covers classifiers, a worked example on public data from 1926 to 2025, evaluation, and the architecture of a production study. §9 is the synthesis. If you read three things, read §1.4 (the reach of a label, and why detection is forecasting), §4.9 (vetting a label before training on it) and §6 (what a causal classifier learns on public data, with labels over a century and classifiers since 1990). Appendix A defines the statistical and financial concepts the main text uses without deriving them.

Relationship to the other notes. Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models supplies three results used throughout: regime models identify volatility and not expected returns; the choice between predicted, filtered and smoothed state estimates governs measured performance; and the effective sample size of any regime study is its number of episodes, not its number of days. It is the prerequisite for §5.7 and §5.8. Implied Volatility derives the VIX and the variance risk premium used in §3.3. Bonds and Bond Markets covers the credit spreads and yield curves of §3.4 and §3.5. Trend-Following in Financial Markets covers the trend estimation behind §2.4. Edge as Information relates hit rates to information, which §1.4 uses to size what a good direction signal delivers. Each note stands alone.

Epistemic tags. Claims are flagged by status where the status changes what you should do:

  • [Fact] — replicated across independent datasets or implementations, with broad agreement among people who have looked.
  • [Contested] — documented, but with live disagreement about magnitude, robustness, or cause.
  • [Hypothesis] — a proposed mechanism, not decisively tested.
  • [Practice] — practitioner convention. It may well be right; the evidence is private or absent, which is not the same as evidence against it.

Untagged sentences are definitions, derivations, or arithmetic. The numbers in §6 and every number attributed to “the worked example” come from public data and are printed by figures/rc_common.py, so you can change a parameter and rerun.

Notation. \(S_t\) is the level of a total-return price index at the close of trading day \(t\), \(r_t = S_t / S_{t-1} - 1\) its simple return and \(\ell_t = \log(1 + r_t)\) its log return. \(A = 252\) is the number of trading days per year. \(\mathcal{F}_t\) is the information available at the close of day \(t\): data published by then, not data that describe day \(t\) but appear later.

\(z_t\) is the vector of latent state variables (§1.3, §2.2): the quantity of risk, the price of risk, the direction of the market, the macroeconomic state and the structure of co-movement. \(x_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the vector of inputs (features) known at \(t\); they relate to the state through \(x_t = \phi(z_t) + \varepsilon_t\), with \(\varepsilon_t\) the measurement noise (§1.3). A regime \(s_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) is a coarse partition of the state, \(s_t = c(z_t)\), into \(K\) classes (coded \(\{0, 1\}\) when \(K = 2\), as for a label). Lowercase \(s_t\) is the regime and uppercase \(S_t\) the price; the two never appear in the same role. As in the companion chapter, vectors such as \(x_t\) and \(z_t\) are set in plain type; \(\Sigma\) denotes a covariance matrix.

A label \(y_t\) is the training target attached to day \(t\), computed from the price path (or from other data) by a rule \(L\): \(y_t = L(S_{t-a}, \dots, S_t, \dots, S_{t+b})\). Its lookback is \(a\) and its reach is \(b\), the number of days after \(t\) on which it depends (§1.4). For a label defined over a forward window of fixed length, \(b = h\), the horizon. Labels are binary unless stated, with \(y_t = 1\) marking the class of interest (the bear market, the high-volatility month). \(p_t = \Pr(y_t = 1 \mid \mathcal{F}_t)\) is the best possible probability forecast of the label, and \(\hat p_t\) a classifier’s estimate of it. An episode is a maximal run of consecutive days with \(y_t = 1\); a label’s episode count is the number of such runs, and an episode’s length the number of days in it.

\(\mathrm{RV}^{(n)}_t = \sqrt{(A/n) \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \ell_{t-i}^2}\) is the trailing \(n\)-day realised volatility, annualised. \(\mathrm{VIX}_t\) is the Cboe volatility index in percentage points. \(\delta\) is the threshold of a turning-point rule (a 20% move unless stated), and \(\tau\) denotes particular dates: a peak, a trough, a confirmation, a refit. \(\Lambda(u) = 1/(1 + e^{-u})\) is the logistic function; \(\sigma\) is reserved for volatility and never means a sigmoid. \(\beta\) collects the coefficients of a classifier and \(\alpha\) the ridge penalty on them (§5.4), \(\lambda\) is the switching penalty of a jump model (§4.6), and \(\kappa\) is Cohen’s kappa (§6.2). AUC, the Brier score \(\mathrm{BS}\) and the Brier skill score \(\mathrm{BSS}\) are defined in §7.1–§7.3 (informally in §1.4 and §5.1). In §5.11, \(p_{jk}\) with two class subscripts is a Markov transition probability, as in the companion chapter; \(p_t\) and \(\hat p_t\), with a time subscript, are label probabilities. A symbol used in one subsection only is defined there.

What you will be able to do. After this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Turn “detect the regime” into a stated decision, a state variable, a label and a horizon, and say in advance how much of the label a classifier can learn.
  2. Choose inputs for each state variable, align them to the time they were published, and transform them so that a model trained on one decade applies to the next.
  3. Construct training labels from six kinds of source, and measure each label’s reach, persistence, stability and episode count before training anything.
  4. Build a walk-forward training set that never uses a label before it was knowable, and score a classifier against the baseline that matters.
  5. Choose among threshold rules, composite indices, logistic models, tree ensembles, latent-state models and teacher–student pipelines for a given decision, and know how each one fails.

1. What classifying a regime means

1.1 The wrong intuition

The intuition most people bring to the problem goes like this. At any moment the market is in some regime: a bull market or a bear market, risk-on or risk-off, calm or stressed. The regime is a fact about the world, like the state of a machine. A good enough model with enough inputs reveals it, and the history of past regimes supplies the training labels. Under this view regime detection is fault detection: more sensors give earlier and surer detection.

The intuition fails in three places.

  1. A regime is a definition, not a fact. Eight reasonable definitions of a “bad” regime on the same century of US data agree only moderately with one another. Their pairwise Cohen’s kappa, a chance-corrected agreement score with 1 for perfect agreement and 0 for agreement no better than chance, ranges from 0.03 to 0.58 for definitions in different families (§6.2). There is no single regime history to recover.
  2. The definitions practitioners care about depend on the future. A day is in a bear market, in the usual sense, only if prices go on to fall 20% from the peak before it. A classifier asked to say so before that fall is complete is being asked to forecast it.
  3. The parts of a regime that are knowable now need measurement, not classification. Today’s volatility, drawdown and credit spread are observable. A rule computes them; nothing has to be learned.

One number makes the second point concrete. Over 1927–2025, a strategy that held the US market when the ±20% bull–bear label said “bull” and cash otherwise earned a Sharpe ratio of 1.54, against 0.45 for holding the market throughout. That uses the label one day ahead. Acting on the label only once the rule itself has confirmed it, the Sharpe ratio was 0.46 (§6.3). In Sharpe-ratio terms, the label’s entire value sits in the days when it cannot yet be known.

The right question is therefore not “which regime are we in?” It is “which property of the coming weeks or months matters to my decision, how well can it be forecast from what I see now, and is a discrete regime the best way to carry that forecast?”

1.2 Three questions before any data

A regime study should begin with a sentence, not a dataset. The sentence answers three questions.

  1. Regime of what? The behaviour of which asset, portfolio or strategy is being classified. A regime of the S&P 500’s volatility, a regime of a momentum strategy’s returns and a regime of the stock–bond correlation are different objects with different inputs.
  2. For which decision? Sizing, hedging, choosing between strategies, setting risk limits, or conditioning another model. The decision says which outcome the label must separate.
  3. At what horizon? The decision’s holding period sets the label’s horizon. A daily volatility-targeting rule needs next-week or next-month risk; a strategic allocation needs the next year’s macroeconomic state.

Written out, a well-posed study reads like this: “Reduce equity exposure when the probability that realised volatility over the next 21 trading days lands in the top fifth of its history exceeds 0.6.” Every term in that sentence is measurable. “Detect the regime” is not.

The decisions fall into three groups, and the groups differ in how much a model can deliver:

Decision Outcome the label must separate Learnable from current data?
Risk: sizing, hedging, limits future volatility, drawdown, correlation largely — risk is persistent (§6.4)
Direction: timing, trend exposure future return, bull or bear phase barely — direction is not identified (§6.4)
Macro allocation: duration, inflation hedges, factor tilts growth, inflation, recession partly — slowly, with lags and revisions (§2.8)

The rest of the chapter elaborates this table. Risk-type regimes are where regime studies earn their keep. Direction-type regimes are where most of them are aimed.

1.3 The master form

Every regime study, whether a VIX threshold or a gradient-boosted classifier trained on jump-model labels, fills the same five slots. In words: a few hidden state variables drive the market; observable inputs measure them with noise; a regime coarsens them into a few classes; a label approximates that coarsening using the realised price path; and a classifier estimates the label from inputs available at the time.

\[ \begin{aligned} x_t &= \phi(z_t) + \varepsilon_t && \text{(inputs observe the state, with noise)} \\[2pt] s_t &= c(z_t) && \text{(a regime is a coarse partition of the state)} \\[2pt] y_t &= L\big(S_{t-a}, \dots, S_t, \dots, S_{t+b}\big) && \text{(a label is computed from the path)} \\[2pt] \hat p_t &= f\big(x_t, x_{t-1}, \dots\big) \approx \Pr\big(y_t = 1 \mid \mathcal{F}_t\big) && \text{(a classifier estimates it causally)} \end{aligned} \]

The state \(z_t\) is continuous and unobserved. §2.2 argues that five state variables underlie every practitioner taxonomy: the quantity of risk (volatility), the price of risk (risk premia and risk appetite), the direction of the market (its conditional mean), the macroeconomic state (growth, inflation and policy), and the structure of co-movement (correlation, dispersion and liquidity). The function \(\phi\) says how inputs relate to these, and \(\varepsilon_t\) is measurement noise: the VIX measures the quantity of risk plus a time-varying premium, a credit spread measures expected default plus the price of risk.

The regime \(s_t = c(z_t)\) is a discretisation. Its value lies in carrying a discrete decision (on or off, strategy A or strategy B) and in communicating; its cost is the information discarded by the coarsening. The label \(y_t\) is the computable stand-in for the regime, the thing a supervised model is trained against. The classifier \(f\) is restricted to inputs dated \(t\) or earlier.

Five slots vary between studies: the state variable, the coarsening \(c\), the label rule \(L\) (including its reach \(b\)), the inputs \(\phi\), and the classifier \(f\). Most named methods are a choice of three of them with the other two left implicit. A VIX-band study chooses the quantity of risk, a coarsening into bands, and a label with zero reach, so it needs no classifier. A bull–bear study chooses direction and a turning-point label, and then usually forgets that the label’s reach is months long. The comparison tables of §2.12, §4.8 and §5.12 are this master form, filled in.

The companion chapter’s master form describes the same objects from the other side. There the regime is a latent Markov state, the “label” is its posterior probability, and nothing is trained against an external target. The two views meet in §5.7 and §5.8: a latent-state model can be the classifier, or it can produce the labels a supervised classifier then learns.

1.4 The reach of a label, and why detection is forecasting

The reach \(b\) of a label is the number of days after \(t\) that the label of day \(t\) depends on. It is the single property that decides what a classifier can learn, how the training set must be built, and how late any detection will be.

First, suppose \(b = 0\). Then \(y_t\) is a function of data available at \(t\), and the best possible forecast is the rule itself: \(p_t \in \{0, 1\}\), and its error is zero. Training a model to reproduce such a label is, at best, a slow way to compute it. “VIX above 30” and “10% below the high” are labels of this kind. They are useful regimes, but they are measured, not learned.

Now suppose \(b > 0\). The label depends on what happens next, and the best possible forecast is the conditional probability \(p_t = \Pr(y_t = 1 \mid \mathcal{F}_t)\). Even this ideal forecaster has an irreducible error. Measured by the Brier score, the mean squared difference between forecast probability and outcome, the ideal forecaster’s error is the expected conditional variance of the label:

\[ \mathrm{BS}^{*} = \mathbb{E}\big[(p_t - y_t)^2\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[p_t\,(1 - p_t)\big]. \]

The second equality is the Bernoulli variance: given \(\mathcal{F}_t\), the squared error is \((1 - p_t)^2\) with probability \(p_t\) and \(p_t^2\) otherwise, so its mean is \(p_t(1 - p_t)\). Hence \(\mathrm{BS}^{*}\) is zero only when \(\mathcal{F}_t\) settles the label, and it is largest when \(p_t\) sits near one half. Whatever a model achieves, in expectation it cannot do better than \(\mathrm{BS}^{*}\), and how large \(\mathrm{BS}^{*}\) is depends on what drives the label’s future part.

This yields the chapter’s first organising claim. A supervised regime “detector” is a forecaster of its label’s future part, and what it can learn is set by what that future part depends on:

  • If the future part is volatility, the label is highly learnable, because volatility is persistent. The log VIX has a daily autocorrelation of 0.98 since 1990, a half-life of about 35 trading days (a deviation with daily autocorrelation \(\rho\) halves in \(\ln 0.5 / \ln \rho\) days). Log 21-day realised volatility on the US market since 1930, regressed on its own value a month earlier, has a slope of 0.72, a half-life of about two months. In §6.4 a label defined by next month’s volatility is forecast with an AUC of 0.88. (AUC is the probability that the classifier ranks a randomly chosen positive day above a randomly chosen negative one; 0.5 is chance.)
  • If the future part is direction, the label is barely learnable. A correlation (an information coefficient) of 0.05 between a forecast and the next period’s return, which would be a good equity-timing signal, corresponds to a hit rate of 51.6% (Edge as Information). In §6.4, a label defined by the sign of the next quarter’s return scores an AUC below 0.5 out of sample.
  • If the future part is the macroeconomic state, the label is learnable at low frequency from slow inputs such as the yield curve and credit spreads, with long publication lags and revisions on both the inputs and the labels.

Detection is forecasting. The usual distinction between “detecting the current regime” and “predicting the next one” disappears once reach is in view. Whatever part of today’s regime is already settled by today’s data can be computed; whatever part is not is a forecast. A study that claims to detect bear markets early is claiming to forecast falls in prices, and must be judged against the evidence on forecasting returns, which is discouraging (Welch & Goyal, 2008).

Random reach. Some labels have no fixed reach. A bull–bear label built from turning points assigns day \(t\) to a bear market if \(t\) lies between a peak and the following trough, where a peak is confirmed only when the price has fallen \(\delta = 20\%\) below it. The label of the days after a peak is therefore settled only on the confirmation date, and its reach is the confirmation lag, the number of days from the turning point to its confirmation. On the US market since 1926 the median confirmation lag was 70 trading days for bear markets (interquartile range 42–146) and 41 for bull markets (§6.3). For about a fifth of all days, the label could not have been known until weeks or months later.

The stale-label baseline. Because labels persist, the most recent label that is fully known at \(t\) is a strong forecast of the current one. For a label with fixed reach \(b\), that is \(y_{t-b}\). For a forward-volatility label with horizon \(h\), \(y_{t-h}\) is computed from the returns of \((t-h, t]\): it is trailing realised volatility compared with a threshold that has barely moved in \(h\) days, a pure persistence forecast. For a turning-point label it is the confirmed state, the rule’s own real-time verdict. A classifier must be judged by its improvement over this stale label, not over the base rate. In §6.4 trailing volatility alone reaches an AUC of 0.84 on the forward-volatility label; the full model adds 0.04.

Two exact equivalences tie these ideas together:

This is exactly Consequence
The real-time ±20% bull–bear rule a hysteresis rule (separate triggers for entering and leaving a state, §5.2): a 20% drawdown from the running peak starts the bear state, a 20% rise from the running trough ends it its “detections” are threshold crossings, made when the move is already 20% deep
The ex-post ±20% bull–bear label the real-time rule with each switch moved back to the preceding peak or trough the two differ only between each turning point and its confirmation: 20% of days since 1927

1.5 Dating, nowcasting and forecasting

Three tasks share the name “regime detection”. They use different information and should be evaluated differently.

Task Information used Example Evaluated against Typical error
Dating the whole sample, before and after \(t\) NBER recession dates, the ex-post bull–bear label, smoothed HMM probabilities historical judgement treating dated labels as observable in real time
Nowcasting \(\mathcal{F}_t\), for a label of day \(t\) “is today in a bear market?”, this week’s financial-conditions index before it is published the label, once settled reporting accuracy on days whose label was already settled
Forecasting \(\mathcal{F}_t\), for a label of a later day “will next month be high-volatility?” the realised label ignoring overlap between consecutive labels

The three tasks correspond to rungs of the filtration ladder in the companion chapter (section 5 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models): dating uses smoothed information, nowcasting filtered information, forecasting predicted information. The most common error in published regime classifiers is to train on dated labels and report accuracy against the same dated labels, as if the accuracy were attainable in real time. It is attainable only on days whose label had already been settled, which are the days where a classifier is least needed.

Nowcasting a label with a long reach is forecasting in disguise. Nowcasting a series that is merely published late is different: the Chicago Fed’s National Financial Conditions Index for the week ending Friday is released the following Wednesday, and estimating it on Monday from daily market data is a measurement problem with a short horizon and a known answer. These are good uses of a supervised model, because the target exists and arrives soon.

§1 Key takeaways

  1. A regime is a definition chosen to serve a decision. Write the decision, the state variable, the label and the horizon in one sentence before touching data.
  2. The reach of a label, the number of future days it depends on, sets what can be learned. A label with zero reach is a rule to compute; a label with positive reach is a forecast.
  3. Supervised regime detection is forecasting of the label’s future part. Labels whose future part is volatility are learnable; labels whose future part is direction are not.
  4. The baseline that matters is the stale label: the most recent fully known label, or the rule’s own confirmed state. Judge every classifier by its improvement over it.
  5. The ex-post bull–bear label and its real-time version differ only between each turning point and its confirmation. That is a fifth of all days, and it is where the label’s value lies.
  6. Dating, nowcasting and forecasting are different tasks. Accuracy measured against dated labels on days already settled says nothing about real-time performance.

2. How practitioners carve up regimes

Practitioners use a dozen regime vocabularies: volatility regimes, bull and bear markets, risk-on and risk-off, stress regimes, business-cycle phases, growth and inflation quadrants, correlation regimes. They look like different ideas. This section argues that they are coarsenings of five state variables, describes each family with the same fields, and shows where the families agree and where they part. The answer to “what kinds of regime can I predict?” falls out of the fields: the families built on the quantity of risk can be forecast, the families built on direction cannot, and the macroeconomic families can be forecast slowly.

2.1 A short lineage

The vocabulary accumulated over a century, and each layer added something a practitioner still uses:

Year Development What changed
1922 W. P. Hamilton’s The Stock Market Barometer sets out Dow theory: primary bull and bear markets, secondary reactions, and confirmation by two averages The first explicit bull–bear taxonomy, with a confirmation lag built into the definition
1946 Burns and Mitchell, Measuring Business Cycles (NBER) Expansions and contractions dated by expert judgement; the official recession dates that most macro labels still use
1971 Bry and Boschan’s turning-point algorithm Dating becomes a reproducible program; its window and minimum-duration parameters become choices
1989 J. D. Hamilton’s Markov-switching model The regime becomes a latent state with probabilities rather than a dated label
2003–04 Pagan and Sossounov; Lunde and Timmermann Price-based bull–bear dating with explicit thresholds
2004–12 The Investment Clock; Bridgewater’s All Weather Allocation by growth–inflation quadrant
2006–19 Financial stress and conditions indices from central banks and the OFR Composite, observable stress regimes published weekly or daily
2018–24 Jump models, clustering, and supervised classifiers trained on model labels Regimes defined by fitted models; classifiers trained to predict them

The record that matters most for this chapter is the first row. A primary bear market in Dow theory exists only once the averages have confirmed it, so the definition practitioners inherited was a lagging one from the start. The econometric strand of this history, from Hamilton’s model onward, is reviewed by Ang and Timmermann (2012).

2.2 Five state variables under every taxonomy

The families below differ in vocabulary, but each one partitions one or two of five continuous state variables. Naming them is the first step to choosing inputs (§3), because inputs are measurements of state variables, not of regimes.

State variable What it is Typical observables Persistence Known at \(t\)?
Quantity of risk the conditional volatility of returns realised volatility, VIX, MOVE high: half-life of one to two months yes, with small error
Price of risk compensation demanded per unit of risk; risk appetite credit spreads, variance risk premium, valuations high partly: a spread is observed, its split into expected loss and premium is not
Direction the conditional mean, or trend trailing returns, distance from moving averages low no: the mean is not identified in short samples
Macroeconomic state growth, inflation, policy stance activity data, inflation, the yield curve, the policy rate very high with publication lags and revisions
Structure how assets move together, and how easily they trade correlations, dispersion, breadth, liquidity measures moderate yes, with estimation noise

The column that decides what can be predicted is the last one, together with persistence. The quantity of risk is observable and persistent, so a regime built on it can be forecast a few weeks ahead with real skill. Direction is neither observable nor persistent, so a regime built on it can be dated in hindsight but hardly forecast. The companion chapter shows the statistical root of this asymmetry: in a fitted regime model, state volatilities are pinned down sixteen times more sharply than state means from the same data (section 8 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models). Most practitioner regimes combine the quantity of risk with direction or with the price of risk. Their observable part is therefore, to a large degree, volatility under another name.

The families that follow are described with the same fields: the idea, the state variables, the definitions in use, typical durations and episodes, whether the regime is observable at \(t\), the decision it serves, its failure modes, and when to use it.

2.3 Volatility regimes

Idea. Classify the market by how much it moves.

State variables. The quantity of risk.

Definitions in use. Bands on the VIX are the commonest: below 15 “calm”, 15–25 “normal”, 25–35 “elevated”, above 35 or 40 “crisis”. These cut points are convention, not estimates [Practice]. Since 1990 the VIX’s median close has been 17.6; it closed below 15 on 32.5% of days, above 30 on 8% and above 40 on 2.3%. Other definitions use quantiles of realised volatility (the top fifth of the history so far), bands on a GARCH volatility estimate, the calm and turbulent states of a two-state hidden Markov model fitted to returns, and composite scores that average standardised measures of the VIX level, its recent change and its own volatility.

Durations and episodes. Long and numerous. In the worked example the label “next month’s realised volatility lands in the top fifth of its history so far” has 166 episodes since 1930, with a median length of 16 days.

Observable at \(t\)? The current level, yes. The level over the coming month, which is what a sizing decision needs, is forecastable with an AUC near 0.88 (§6.4).

Decision. Position sizing and volatility targeting, option strategy selection, stop and limit widths, risk budgets.

Failure modes.

  • Non-stationary levels. A VIX of 20 was a calm reading in 2002, when the index averaged 27, and an alarming one in 2017, when it averaged 11. Fixed bands misclassify whole years.
  • Rolling normalisation turns a level into a surprise. A score built from a rolling z-score over, say, a year adapts to the level it is measuring. After a year at a VIX of 35 the score reads “normal”. Such a score classifies the change in risk, which is a different regime from the level of risk, and a sizing rule needs the level. Use long expanding windows or percentiles against the history so far for levels, and reserve short-window z-scores for explicitly measuring surprise (§3.12).
  • Implied is not realised. The VIX contains a variance risk premium that varies with the price of risk (§3.3), so a VIX band mixes two state variables.
  • A volatility regime is not a direction regime. High volatility also contains the best days of each decade, which cluster in rebounds. Volatility timing earns its keep by reducing risk, not by avoiding losses. [Contested] Whether it also improves returns out of sample is disputed (Moreira & Muir, 2017; Cederburg et al., 2020).

When to use it. Whenever the decision is about risk. It is the default regime, and the only family for which forecasts are reliably better than the stale label.

2.4 Trend regimes: bull, bear, correction, rebound

Idea. Classify the market by the direction and persistence of its price path.

State variables. Direction, with the quantity of risk entering because bear markets are volatile.

Definitions in use. Five constructions are common.

  1. The ±20% rule. A bear market runs from a peak to the following trough, where the peak is followed by a fall of at least 20% and the trough by a rise of at least 20%. The financial press uses it; Lunde and Timmermann (2004) formalised it with separate thresholds for the two directions. A fall of 10% to 20% is a correction.
  2. Business-cycle dating applied to prices. Pagan and Sossounov (2003) adapted the Bry–Boschan algorithm to monthly stock prices: find local maxima and minima, enforce alternation, censor the ends of the sample, and require a minimum cycle of 16 months and a minimum phase of four months unless the move exceeds 20%.
  3. Trailing-return states. Cooper, Gutierrez and Hameed (2004) call the market UP when its return over the past 36 months is non-negative. Daniel and Moskowitz (2016) mark a bear state when the past two years’ cumulative return is negative.
  4. Moving-average states. The price is above or below its 200-day or ten-month average (Faber, 2007).
  5. Four-phase cycles. Goulding, Harvey and Mazzoleni (2023) cross the signs of a slow (12-month) and a fast (1-month) time-series momentum signal: Bull when both are positive, Bear when both are negative, Correction when the slow signal is positive and the fast one negative, Rebound when the reverse. Maheu, McCurdy and Song (2012) fit a four-state Markov-switching model with bull, bull-correction, bear and bear-rally states.

Durations and episodes. Few. The ±20% rule finds 31 bear markets on the US total market since 1926, nine of them since 2000, with a median length of about six months (128 trading days on the common sample of §6.2; §6.3 lists those since 2000). Longer histories add episodes: Gonzalez, Powell, Shi and Wilson (2005) date two centuries of US bull and bear cycles.

Observable at \(t\)? The ex-post definitions (1 and 2) are not: their reach is the confirmation lag, a median of 70 trading days for bear markets. The trailing definitions (3, 4 and 5) are observable, because they are rules with zero reach. They are trend signals rather than forecasts, and the trend-following literature is where their value is assessed (Trend-Following in Financial Markets).

Decision. Market exposure; the risk of momentum strategies, whose crashes cluster in bear states with high volatility, when the market rebounds (Daniel & Moskowitz, 2016); the choice of trend speed (Goulding, Harvey & Mazzoleni, 2023).

Failure modes.

  • Thresholds and index choice flip borderline episodes. The S&P 500 price index fell 19.9% in 1990, 19.3% in 1998, 19.4% in 2011 and 19.8% in 2018: no bear market by the press convention. The total US market including dividends and small companies fell more than 20% in all four, so each is a bear market in the worked example. Four of its eleven bear markets since 1990 exist or not depending on the index.
  • Bear-market rallies count as bull markets. The US market rose more than 20% between late November 2008 and early January 2009 before falling to new lows, so the ±20% rule records a brief bull market in the middle of the financial crisis. Four-phase definitions exist to repair this.
  • The confirmation lag. By construction, the rule recognises a bear market once prices are 20% below the peak.
  • Censoring. The last phase of any sample is provisional; its end is unknown.

When to use it. For describing history and for benchmarks. As a training target only if the decision really needs direction and the limit on learning direction set out in §1.4 is accepted.

2.5 Trending versus mean-reverting markets

Idea. Classify the market by whether it extends moves or reverses them.

State variables. The persistence of direction: the autocorrelation of returns at the strategy’s horizon.

Definitions in use. The variance ratio \(\mathrm{VR}(q)\), the variance of \(q\)-day returns divided by \(q\) times the variance of one-day returns, above one for trending and below one for mean-reverting markets (Lo & MacKinlay, 1988); the Hurst exponent; the autocorrelation of daily returns; and practitioner indicators such as the efficiency ratio (net move divided by path length) and the average directional index [Practice].

Durations and episodes. Short and noisy.

Observable at \(t\)? Only with large error. An autocorrelation estimated from 63 days of returns has a standard error of about \(1/\sqrt{63} \approx 0.13\), larger than the variation in autocorrelation the regime is meant to detect.

Decision. Choosing between trend-following and mean-reversion strategies; placing stops and targets.

Failure modes. Noise dominates. The P&L of a trend rule depends on the autocorrelation of returns at its own horizon over the holding period, which is a forecast of direction’s persistence, not a measurement of it (Trend-Following in Financial Markets).

When to use it. As a descriptive statistic over long windows. There is little out-of-sample support for switching strategies on short-window estimates [Practice].

2.6 Risk-on and risk-off

Idea. On some days and in some periods risky assets rise together while havens fall (risk-on); in others the reverse (risk-off).

State variables. The price of risk, at a global level, and structure.

Definitions in use. The sign or standardised size of a common factor in cross-asset returns, usually the first principal component (the single weighted average of the returns that carries the most common variation) of equities, credit, emerging markets, commodities and carry currencies against Treasuries, gold, the yen, the Swiss franc and the dollar. Chari, Dilts Stedman and Lundblad (2023) build a risk-on/risk-off index from several market-based measures. Miranda-Agrippino and Rey (2020) find a single global factor behind a large share of the variation in risky-asset prices worldwide. Bekaert, Hoerova and Lo Duca (2013) split the VIX into risk aversion and uncertainty.

Durations and episodes. The daily sign flips often; the strength of the common factor, its share of cross-asset variance over a rolling window, persists for weeks to months.

Observable at \(t\)? Yes. It describes today’s co-movement.

Decision. Cross-asset hedging, the risk of carry trades and of emerging-market exposure.

Failure modes. The definition is close to circular: a risk-off day is a day on which risky assets fell. The set of havens changes; Treasuries hedged equities from about 2000 to 2021 and did not in 2022 (§2.9). A daily sign is not a regime: use the rolling strength of the factor, or its smoothed level.

When to use it. For multi-asset portfolios, as a structure measure rather than a forecast.

2.7 Financial stress and liquidity

Idea. The financial system either functions normally, or funding and market liquidity are impaired and prices are driven by forced selling.

State variables. The price of risk and structure. In stress, correlations rise and diversification fails.

Definitions in use. Composite indices published by public institutions:

  • The St. Louis Fed Financial Stress Index (STLFSI4) combines 18 weekly series (seven interest rates, six yield spreads and five other indicators) through their first principal component. Its average since late 1993 is zero, so positive values mean above-average stress (Kliesen & Smith, 2010).
  • The Chicago Fed National Financial Conditions Index (NFCI) is a weighted average of 105 indicators of risk, credit and leverage, with weights from a dynamic factor model. It is scaled to mean zero and standard deviation one since 1971, and positive values mean tighter-than-average conditions (Brave & Butters, 2012). An adjusted version (ANFCI) removes the part explained by economic activity and inflation.
  • The OFR Financial Stress Index combines 33 daily market indicators in five categories (credit, equity valuation, funding, safe assets and volatility). It is zero at normal stress, and once estimated its values do not change (Monin, 2019).
  • The ECB’s CISS weights its sub-indices by their cross-correlations, so that stress counts for more when it is systemic, spreading across markets at once (Hollo, Kremer & Lo Duca, 2012).
  • Turbulence, the squared Mahalanobis distance of today’s cross-asset returns from their historical mean (§5.3; Kritzman & Li, 2010), and the absorption ratio, the share of variance explained by the leading eigenvectors (Kritzman, Li, Page & Rigobon, 2011), are market-only constructions in the same spirit.

Common cut points are zero (above-average stress), and one and two standard deviations for “significant” and “severe” stress [Practice].

Durations and episodes. Weeks to months, and few systemic episodes: in the US since 1990, roughly 1998, 2001–02, 2007–09, 2011, 2020 and a handful of shorter ones.

Observable at \(t\)? Yes for the daily market-based indices, after a lag of a day or two (the OFR index publishes two business days late); with a longer lag for the weekly ones, whose readings for the week ending Friday appear the following Wednesday.

Decision. Leverage, liquidity buffers, risk limits, and whether to trust a diversification assumption.

Failure modes.

  • Revisions. The NFCI is re-estimated every week, so its history changes. The Chicago Fed describes the changes as usually small, but a backtest on today’s history uses weights that were not available then.
  • Full-sample weights. Weights estimated on the whole sample and applied to its early years carry information from later crises into earlier readings.
  • Composition changes. The STLFSI was rebuilt as LIBOR was retired: its LIBOR-based spreads gave way to SOFR-based ones, and version 4 replaced a backward-looking 90-day average SOFR with the forward-looking 90-day rate.
  • Conditions are not stress. The NFCI includes leverage measures, which build slowly in good times; a stress index measures acute strain. The two answer different questions.

Evidence. The NFCI predicts episodes of financial stress at horizons up to a year (Brave & Butters, 2012), and financial conditions forecast the lower tail of GDP growth much better than its median (Adrian, Boyarchenko & Giannone, 2019).

When to use it. For risk limits and leverage, and as a compact input that summarises dozens of series (§3.6).

2.8 Macroeconomic regimes

Idea. Classify periods by the state of the economy, on the theory that asset classes respond to it in understandable ways.

State variables. The macroeconomic state: growth, inflation and policy.

Definitions in use. Four variants.

  1. The business cycle. NBER expansions and recessions are the reference. Real-time alternatives include Markov-switching dynamic-factor models of activity (Chauvet & Piger, 2008), the Sahm rule, which signals a recession when the three-month average unemployment rate rises half a percentage point above its low of the previous twelve months (Sahm, 2019), and probit models on the yield curve (Estrella & Mishkin, 1998). Hamilton (2011) surveys how such methods have performed in real time, and Giusto and Piger (2017) date turning points in real time with a simple machine-learning classifier, vector quantisation. Composite leading indicators such as the OECD’s are usually read in four phases by crossing the indicator’s level relative to its trend with its direction: above trend and rising, above and falling, below and falling, below and rising [Practice] (OECD, 2012).
  2. Growth–inflation quadrants. Bridgewater’s All Weather framework defines four environments by whether growth and inflation are rising or falling relative to expectations, and holds assets that suit each, balanced by risk (Podolsky, Johnson & Jennings, 2012). Merrill Lynch’s Investment Clock names four phases from the direction of growth and inflation: reflation, recovery, overheat and stagflation (Greetham and colleagues, Merrill Lynch, 2004). These are practitioner frameworks from firms that sell allocation products built on them.
  3. Statistical macro-market regimes. A Gaussian mixture fitted to 17 factor returns from 1971 to 2020 yields four conditions named Crisis, Steady State, Inflation and Walking on Ice (Botte & Bao, 2021). Guidolin and Timmermann (2007) find four states for stocks and bonds jointly: crash, slow growth, bull and recovery.
  4. Monetary-policy regimes. Hiking, cutting and holding cycles, measured by the six- to twelve-month change in the policy rate or the two-year yield, and the zero-rate period as its own regime.

Durations and episodes. Years, and very few. The US has had 12 recessions since 1948. Inflation regimes number a handful.

Observable at \(t\)? Only with publication lags and revisions. NBER dates are not observable in real time at all: the committee announced peaks an average of 7.3 months after they occurred, and troughs 15 months after, over the cycles since 1978 (NBER announcements). The trough of March 1991 was announced in December 1992.

Decision. Strategic allocation, duration and inflation hedging, factor tilts.

Failure modes.

  • Few episodes. Twelve recessions is the whole post-war sample for a recession classifier.
  • Revisions. Real-time and final macroeconomic data differ, sometimes enough to change the sign of a growth reading (Croushore & Stark, 2001).
  • Two-sided filters. A detrended indicator built with the Hodrick–Prescott filter, as the OECD’s composite leading indicators have been since 2008, revises its recent values as new data arrive (Hamilton, 2018).
  • Relationships break. The 10-year minus 3-month Treasury spread was negative from late October 2022 to mid-December 2024, the longest inversion on record, and no NBER recession had followed at the time of writing.

When to use it. For slow allocation decisions, with labels lagged by their publication delay. Rarely for daily equity decisions, where macro data move too slowly to help except through surprises on release days (§3.10).

2.9 Correlation and dispersion regimes

Idea. Classify periods by how assets move together, not by how much they move.

State variables. Structure.

Definitions in use.

  • The stock–bond correlation. Negative from the late 1990s to about 2020, positive before that and again from 2021–22. Its sign appears to track whether inflation shocks or growth shocks dominate (Campbell, Sunderam & Viceira, 2017); macroeconomic fundamentals explain little of its variation, and liquidity factors more (Baele, Bekaert & Inghelbrecht, 2010). For a balanced portfolio it is the most consequential regime of all (section 14 of Bonds and Bond Markets).
  • Equity correlation. The average correlation among index members, or the implied correlation from index and single-stock options (Cboe’s COR1M and COR3M indices, with history from 2006). [Contested] Average correlation predicts market returns, because it tracks aggregate risk (Pollet & Wilson, 2010), and correlation risk carries a premium in index options (Driessen, Maenhout & Vilkov, 2009).
  • Dispersion. The cross-sectional spread of stock returns separates a “macro” market from a “stock-picker’s” market, and is linked to time variation in the value and momentum premiums (Stivers & Sun, 2010).

Durations and episodes. The stock–bond sign changes every decade or two: very few episodes. Equity correlation regimes last weeks to months.

Observable at \(t\)? Yes, with estimation noise. A correlation estimated over 63 days has a standard error of roughly \((1 - \rho^2)/\sqrt{63}\), about 0.11 at \(\rho = 0.3\). Correlations measured in volatile periods are also biased upward for mechanical reasons (Forbes & Rigobon, 2002).

Decision. Diversification and hedge ratios; dispersion trades; factor exposure.

Failure modes. Estimation noise; the volatility bias; and, for the stock–bond sign, a sample of two or three regimes in a century.

When to use it. Whenever a portfolio relies on a correlation. It is the regime most often ignored and most often decisive.

2.10 Calendar and event regimes

Some regimes are known in advance: Federal Reserve announcement days, the release days of inflation and employment data, monthly options expiry, quarter ends, earnings seasons, holidays. Volatility and volume behave differently on them. They should enter a study as features, never as something to detect. Leaving them out has a cost: a classifier that does not know a release is scheduled may read the release-day spike in volatility as the start of a regime.

2.11 How the families overlap, and where they part

The families overlap because volatility rises when prices fall. Low volatility, bull markets, risk-on, low stress and expansions tend to occur together. The overlap is real but partial. In the worked example’s century of US data, the chance-corrected agreement between the ex-post bear-market label and the next-month high-volatility label is \(\kappa = 0.35\), between either and NBER recessions about 0.3, and between the rule’s own real-time bear state and a negative next quarter 0.03 (§6.2).

The episodes where the families part are the informative ones. The table uses the worked example’s data: the US total market, the VIX and the Baa–Treasury credit spread.

Episode Largest drawdown in the window VIX Baa – 10-year spread, start → high NBER recession Families that fired
Aug–Dec 1987 33.1% not yet published 2.0 → 2.7 points no volatility, trend; no macro
Jan–Jun 2007 5.9% mean 13, high 20 flat near 1.6 no almost none; the yield curve was inverted
Jul–Dec 2007 9.7% mean 22, high 31 1.6 → 2.6 points no (the peak was December) credit and stress before equity
Sep–Dec 2018 20.4% high 36 1.9 → 2.5 points no trend, volatility; mild credit
Feb–Apr 2020 34.2% high 83 2.1 → 4.3 points yes all of them, briefly
Jan–Oct 2022 25.4% mean 26, high 36.5 1.8 → 2.4 points no trend; stock–bond correlation turned positive
Feb–Apr 2025 19.6% high 52 1.5 → 2.0 points no volatility; trend on some indices

Two lessons follow. First, a single “regime” label hides which family fired, and the families call for different responses: the credit-led stress of late 2007 called for cutting leverage while equity volatility was still moderate, and the 2022 bear market called for hedges other than Treasuries. Second, the borderline cases decide the labels: 2025 is a bear market on some indices (the Nasdaq Composite fell more than 20%) and not on the total market, which fell 19.6%, and the decision a study takes on such cases shapes everything trained on them.

2.12 The taxonomy as a product space

The families are coordinates in the master form of §1.3, not branches of a tree:

Family State variable Usual \(K\) Usual dating Reach of the usual label US episodes Decision
Volatility quantity of risk 2–4 threshold or quantile 0 (level) or 21 days (forward) over a hundred sizing, risk
Bull–bear direction 2–4 turning points median 70 days for bear onsets 31 since 1926 exposure
Trending vs mean-reverting direction’s persistence 2 rolling statistic 0 (estimated) noisy strategy choice
Risk-on/off price of risk, structure 2 factor sign or strength 0 many, short cross-asset hedging
Stress price of risk, structure 2–3 composite index 0, plus publication lag about ten leverage, limits
Business cycle macro 2–4 expert or model months to years 12 since 1948 allocation
Growth–inflation macro 4 sign of changes months a handful allocation
Correlation structure 2 rolling estimate 0 (estimated) 2–3 for stock–bond diversification

Which axis matters. The state variable chosen determines what can be forecast far more than the details of the definition. Within a family, thresholds change the episode count a great deal and the labels much less: moving from ±20% to ±15% raises the number of bear markets from 31 to 47, yet the two labels agree with \(\kappa = 0.88\). Across families, agreement falls to between 0.03 and 0.58. Spend design effort on choosing the state variable and the horizon; tune thresholds last.

§2 Key takeaways

  1. Practitioner regimes are coarsenings of five state variables: the quantity of risk, the price of risk, direction, the macroeconomic state and structure. Name the state variable before choosing inputs.
  2. Regimes built on the quantity of risk are observable and persistent, so they can be forecast. Regimes built on direction can be dated in hindsight and hardly forecast. Macro regimes move slowly and arrive late.
  3. The ±20% bull–bear convention is index-dependent at the margin: four of the eleven bear markets on the total US market since 1990 were not bear markets on the S&P 500 price index.
  4. Stress and conditions indices are good compact inputs, but the weekly ones are revised and use full-sample weights. Prefer indices that are not revised, or store the vintages.
  5. Macro regimes have a dozen episodes and labels published months late. Lag them by their real announcement delay or do not use them.
  6. The families overlap because volatility rises when prices fall, and they part in exactly the episodes that matter. Keep them as separate outputs rather than merging them into one label.
  7. Thresholds move episode counts more than they move labels. Choose the state variable and horizon first; tune thresholds last.

3. Inputs: observing the state variables

An input is useful to a regime classifier only through what it says about a state variable. This section goes through the input families by the state variable they measure, gives each one’s mechanism, history and failure modes, and ends with the two practical problems that decide whether any of it works: aligning inputs to the time they became known, and transforming them so that a relationship estimated in one decade holds in the next. The section’s conclusion, borne out by the worked example, is that the input space is much smaller than the list of series suggests: two factors carry most of the variation, and the price path itself carries most of the information.

3.1 What makes a good regime input

Six properties, in rough order of importance:

  1. Mechanism. A reason the input moves with the state variable the label depends on. A credit spread widens with the price of default risk; the VIX rises with expected volatility. An input with no mechanism is a specification search waiting to happen.
  2. History. Enough history to contain many episodes of the regime. An input that starts in 2009 has never seen 2008, and in the worked example a model that gained a new input but lost nineteen years of history did worse (§6.4).
  3. Timeliness. Published soon after the fact, at a frequency at least as high as the decision’s. A monthly series cannot inform a daily decision except on release days.
  4. Point-in-time integrity. Never revised, or revised with stored vintages. A revised series used at its latest vintage leaks future information into the past.
  5. Stationarity, or a transform that delivers it. A level that drifts across decades must be converted into something comparable over time (§3.12).
  6. Non-redundancy. Information beyond the inputs already present. Most candidate inputs are noisy measurements of the volatility factor (§3.13).

Recommendation. Rank candidate inputs by these properties before testing any of them. Testing forty inputs against a label with thirty episodes finds something every time, and the something does not survive.

3.2 The price path itself

What it measures. The quantity of risk and the direction, directly.

The inputs. Realised volatility over several horizons (5, 21 and 63 days), the downside semivariance, the drawdown from the running or one-year high, trailing returns over one, three and twelve months, the distance from moving averages, realised skewness, and jump measures. With intraday data, realised variance from five-minute returns is a far more precise volatility measurement than a daily-return estimate (Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold & Labys, 2003), and the heterogeneous autoregression of daily, weekly and monthly realised variance is the standard forecasting model built on it (Corsi, 2009).

Why they come first. They are available for the longest history, they are never revised, and they measure the two state variables most labels depend on. In the worked example, seven price-path features alone reached an AUC of 0.87 for next month’s volatility and 0.83 for the ex-post bear-market label, and no other input set beat them by more than 0.01 (§6.4).

Failure modes. Price-path features of direction (trailing returns, distance from averages) are rules with zero reach. They describe the trend that has happened; any forecasting value they have is the time-series momentum effect, with its own literature and its own crashes (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen, 2012).

3.3 The implied-volatility complex

What it measures. The quantity of risk expected by option buyers, plus the premium they pay for it.

The inputs.

  • The VIX, the 30-day model-free implied volatility of the S&P 500, with history from 1990 (Cboe VIX methodology). Its square is the risk-neutral expectation of the next month’s variance, which equals the physical expectation plus the variance risk premium (sections 5 and 6 of Implied Volatility).
  • The VIX term structure. Cboe publishes 9-day (VIX9D, from 2011), 3-month (VIX3M; its free history file starts in September 2009) and 6-month (VIX6M, from 2008) indices. The ratio of the VIX to the VIX3M is normally below one; above one, the curve is inverted, which marks acute stress. It was inverted on 7.7% of days from September 2009 to 2025, in 99 separate spells. The slope carries information about the returns of volatility assets, such as variance swaps and VIX futures (Johnson, 2017; Simon & Campasano, 2014).
  • The variance risk premium: the VIX squared minus a forecast of realised variance, often proxied by trailing realised variance. [Contested] It predicts equity returns, most strongly at about a quarter’s horizon (Bollerslev, Tauchen & Zhou, 2009). Splitting the VIX into the premium and the expected variance, the premium predicts returns and the expected variance predicts economic activity and financial instability (Bekaert & Hoerova, 2014) [Contested] on magnitude and stability.
  • Volatility of volatility and tails. The VVIX (the VIX of the VIX, from 2006) and the SKEW index (the price of S&P 500 tail protection, from 1990). Evidence that the SKEW anticipates crashes is weak; it measures demand for protection, which is high in calm, complacent markets as well as before falls [Contested].
  • Cross-asset implied volatility. The MOVE index of Treasury implied volatility, crude oil (OVX), gold (GVZ), the Nasdaq-100 (VXN) and the Russell 2000 (RVX), and implied volatility on credit ETFs. These measure the quantity of risk in other markets and help when the label is about those markets.

Why it matters. The VIX is forward-looking where realised volatility is backward-looking. In the worked example the VIX alone forecast next month’s volatility better than trailing realised volatility alone, with an AUC of 0.87 against 0.84 (§6.4).

Failure modes.

  • Non-stationary levels (§2.3).
  • A premium that moves. The VIX mixes expected volatility with the price of volatility risk; when the premium jumps, a VIX band misreads expected risk.
  • Flicker in term-structure ratios. Ninety-nine inversion spells in sixteen years is a signal that switches on and off within days. Use a smoothed ratio or hysteresis.
  • Short histories. Every term-structure input except the VIX itself starts after 2005 in free data, so a model that relies on them is trained on two or three stress episodes.

3.4 Credit

What it measures. The price of default risk, and through it the price of risk in general.

The inputs.

  • Moody’s Baa yield minus the 10-year Treasury yield, daily on FRED from 1986 (series BAA10Y). Long-history monthly versions extend the comparison back much further.
  • Option-adjusted spreads of the ICE BofA high-yield and investment-grade indices. Since April 2026 FRED publishes only a rolling three-year window of these, so a long history has to be stored as it is fetched or bought.
  • The Gilchrist–Zakrajšek credit spread and the excess bond premium, the part of corporate spreads not explained by expected default. The premium predicts economic activity better than the spread itself (Gilchrist & Zakrajšek, 2012); the Federal Reserve publishes it monthly from 1973 (Favara, Gilchrist, Lewis & Zakrajšek, 2016).
  • Credit ETF prices and options: high-yield and investment-grade bond funds, the ratio of a high-yield fund to a Treasury fund, and implied volatility on the high-yield fund.

Mechanism. A spread is expected default loss plus a risk premium plus a liquidity premium (sections 8 and 9 of Bonds and Bond Markets). The premium component moves with the price of risk, which is why credit can lead equity: in the second half of 2007 the Baa spread widened by a full percentage point while the stock market’s largest fall was under 10% (§2.11).

Failure modes. Composition drift: index ratings mixes and durations change over decades. Level shifts across eras: a Baa spread of 2.5 points was a stress reading in 2018 and an ordinary one in parts of the 1980s. Duration mismatch: the Baa yield refers to long bonds, compared here with a 10-year Treasury.

3.5 Rates and the yield curve

What it measures. The macroeconomic state and expected policy.

The inputs. The 10-year minus 3-month Treasury spread (daily from 1982), the 10-year minus 2-year spread, the near-term forward spread, real yields and breakeven inflation rates from inflation-protected Treasuries, the 2-year yield as a proxy for expected policy, and the MOVE index.

Evidence. The term spread is the best single predictor of recessions two to six quarters ahead (Estrella & Hardouvelis, 1991; Estrella & Mishkin, 1998) [Fact] for the post-war sample. A systematic comparison of leading indicators finds the term spread strongest four to six quarters ahead, with its recent path and broker-dealer margin balances adding information at other horizons (Liu & Moench, 2016). The spread between the expected short rate six quarters ahead and the current short rate is a cleaner version of the signal (Engstrom & Sharpe, 2019).

For equity regimes. The curve is slow. In the worked example the 10-year minus 3-month spread was nearly uncorrelated with the volatility inputs (correlation 0.05 with the log VIX) and added nothing to daily classifiers (§3.13, §6.4).

Failure modes. The relationship rests on eight or so recessions since the 1960s, and its latest signal has not been followed by one so far: the inversion from October 2022 to December 2024 was the longest on record (§2.8). The slope mixes expected policy with a term premium that quantitative easing compressed, and the zero lower bound pinned the short end from 2009 to 2015.

3.6 Composite stress and conditions indices

What they measure. The price of risk and structure, summarised from dozens of series.

The inputs. The STLFSI4 and NFCI (weekly), the OFR Financial Stress Index (daily), and the ECB’s CISS for the euro area (§2.7). Each is a factor model that someone else maintains: it compresses many spreads, rates and volatilities into one number.

Use them with three precautions. Lag each index to its publication date: weekly readings for the week ending Friday are released the following Wednesday. Prefer indices that are not revised, such as the OFR index, or store the vintages of those that are, such as the NFCI (FRED’s archival service, ALFRED, keeps them). And remember that weights estimated on the full sample make the index’s early history partly hindsight.

3.7 Breadth and market internals

What they measure. Structure: how widely a move is shared.

The inputs. The share of index members above their 50- and 200-day moving averages; the advance–decline line; new 52-week highs minus new lows; up and down volume; the NYSE TICK (stocks trading on an uptick minus those on a downtick, intraday); the Arms index or TRIN; and ratios of equal-weight to cap-weight indices, small to large companies, and cyclical to defensive sectors.

Mechanism. Narrowing participation is held to precede market tops, and broad “breadth thrusts” to follow bottoms [Practice].

Evidence. Breadth and similar sentiment measures move strongly with contemporaneous returns but have little power to predict near-term returns (Brown & Cliff, 2004).

Failure modes.

  • Survivorship. Breadth computed from today’s index members excludes the stocks that were removed after falling. Historical breadth then looks healthier than it was in every downturn, and a classifier trained on it learns a false relationship. Use point-in-time membership, or treat the bias as known and avoid breadth levels.
  • Data quality. Exchange-published breadth series have gaps and definitional changes; derived series need consistent universes.
  • Noise. TICK and TRIN are intraday microstructure measures. At daily horizons they are dominated by noise.

3.8 Correlation, dispersion and cross-asset structure

What they measure. Structure, and through it the price of risk.

The inputs. The average pairwise correlation of index members, or each member’s correlation with the index, over one to three months; implied correlation (COR1M and COR3M); the cross-sectional dispersion of returns; the rolling stock–bond correlation; turbulence and the absorption ratio (§2.7); and the strength of a cross-asset risk factor (§2.6).

Evidence. Average correlation predicts market returns (Pollet & Wilson, 2010), and correlation risk is priced in index options (Driessen, Maenhout & Vilkov, 2009). Turbulence and the absorption ratio rise before and during systemic episodes (Kritzman & Li, 2010; Kritzman, Li, Page & Rigobon, 2011) [Contested]: the authors’ firm sells analytics built on them, and the evidence is largely in-sample.

Failure modes. Estimation noise (§2.9). The volatility bias: correlation rises mechanically with volatility, so a correlation regime can be a volatility regime in disguise (Forbes & Rigobon, 2002). Survivorship in member-based measures, as with breadth.

3.9 Sentiment and positioning

What they measure. The price of risk as revealed by what investors pay for protection or how they are positioned.

The inputs. Put/call volume ratios: the equity ratio, dominated by trading in single-stock options; the index ratio, dominated by institutional hedging and structurally near or above one; and the total. Survey sentiment (the American Association of Individual Investors’ weekly survey), futures positioning reported by the CFTC, margin debt, fund flows, and composite indices such as that of Baker and Wurgler (2006).

Evidence. Extreme readings of the VIX, the put/call ratio and TRIN have been found to have contrarian predictive power for S&P 500 futures returns (Simon & Wiggins, 2001). Other work finds that such sentiment measures are caused by past returns and volatility and add little once those are controlled for (Wang, Keswani & Taylor, 2006). Where option volume does predict returns, the information is in the volume of buyers opening new positions, which is not public; the public ratios do not carry it (Pan & Poteshman, 2006). The evidence for public sentiment measures as regime inputs is [Contested] at best.

Structural breaks. The composition of option volume has changed enough to break the comparability of put/call ratios over time. Retail option trading grew sharply from 2020 (Bryzgalova, Pavlova & Sikorskaya, 2023), and options expiring the same day grew from a small fraction of S&P 500 index option volume a decade ago to more than 60% in May 2025 (Cboe, 2025). A level of the index put/call ratio in 2025 does not mean what the same level meant in 2015.

Recommendation. If you use sentiment inputs, use them as residuals: regress each on recent returns and volatility, and keep what those do not explain. Then test the residual against the price-path baseline. Expect little.

3.10 Macroeconomic data

What it measures. The macroeconomic state.

The inputs. Weekly initial unemployment claims; monthly payrolls, purchasing managers’ indices, industrial production and retail sales; composite activity indices such as the Chicago Fed National Activity Index, and the daily business-conditions index of Aruoba, Diebold and Scotti (2009); inflation measures; and surprise indices, which standardise each release’s deviation from the consensus forecast and aggregate across releases (Scotti, 2016). Any economic calendar that records consensus forecasts alongside actual values supports a surprise index.

Real time. Macro data are revised, sometimes heavily, and the vintage available on a date differs from today’s history (Croushore & Stark, 2001). Daily nowcasting models update an estimate of the current quarter as each release arrives (Giannone, Reichlin & Small, 2008).

For equity regimes. Macro data move the slow regimes of §2.8. For daily equity classification they matter mainly through surprises on release days.

3.11 Information timing

A daily regime study joins series that are observed at different times, published with different lags, and revised on different schedules. The join is where most regime studies leak. The rule is simple to state: align every input to the time it became available, not to the date it describes.

Input Describes Usable from Revised?
Index closes, VIX family the trading day that day’s close no
Treasury yields and the Baa spread (FRED) a business day the next business day no
ICE BofA option-adjusted spreads (FRED) a business day the next morning no
NFCI, STLFSI4 the week ending Friday the following Wednesday NFCI weekly; check vintages
OFR Financial Stress Index a business day two business days later no
Cboe put/call ratios the trading day that evening, after the close no
Initial claims the week ending Saturday the following Thursday yes
Payrolls, CPI the month the following month payrolls twice, then annually; CPI rarely
NBER turning points a month 4 to 21 months later rarely
Breadth from index members the trading day that day survivorship unless point-in-time

Four rules follow:

  1. Lag to publication. Shift each series by its release lag before joining it to the price data.
  2. Store what you fetched, when you fetched it. A store that overwrites history with the latest vintage destroys the evidence of what was known.
  3. Forward-fill weekly and monthly series from their release date, never from their reference date.
  4. Never normalise with full-sample statistics. A z-score that uses the full-sample mean and standard deviation carries the future into every past value.

3.12 Transforming inputs

Raw levels rarely survive a change of decade. A model trained when the VIX averaged 27 and applied when it averages 11 extrapolates. Transforms make inputs comparable across time:

  • Logs for volatilities and ratios of volatilities. The log VIX is closer to symmetric and mean-reverting than the VIX itself.
  • Ratios and differences for term structures (VIX/VIX3M) and for the gap between implied and realised volatility.
  • Changes over one to three months for slow-moving levels such as spreads and the curve.
  • Percentiles or z-scores against an expanding window for levels whose meaning should be absolute: a VIX in the top decile of all history is high whatever the last year was like.
  • Z-scores against a rolling window only for inputs whose meaning is relative to recent experience. A rolling z-score measures surprise. Applied to a persistent level it erases the level, and a regime score built that way classifies changes in risk rather than risk (§2.3).
  • Clipping at four or five standard deviations, so that one crisis does not dominate the fit and a new crisis does not produce an absurd extrapolation.

Every transform must be causal: computed from data up to \(t\) only. An expanding quantile threshold satisfies this; a full-sample quantile does not.

3.13 How many independent inputs are there?

Fewer than the list suggests. On daily data from September 2009 to 2025, seven standardised inputs (the log VIX, log 21-day realised volatility, the log VIX/VIX3M ratio, the Baa spread, the 10-year minus 3-month spread, the drawdown from the one-year high, and the distance from the 200-day average) have a first principal component that explains 54% of their joint variance and a second that explains 22%. On the six with history back to 1990, the shares are 62% and 19%. The correlations show the structure:

log VIX log RV VIX/VIX3M Baa spread 10y–3m drawdown trend
log VIX 1.00
log realised vol 0.81 1.00
VIX/VIX3M 0.68 0.55 1.00
Baa spread 0.32 0.29 0.12 1.00
10y–3m spread 0.05 −0.03 0.01 0.58 1.00
drawdown 0.74 0.75 0.57 0.22 −0.12 1.00
trend −0.52 −0.60 −0.48 −0.28 0.05 −0.85 1.00

Two clusters stand out: a fast volatility and drawdown factor (VIX, realised volatility, term structure, drawdown, trend) and a slow credit and curve factor. Adding a twentieth series usually adds a noisier measurement of the first factor, not a new dimension.

Recommendation. Build one or two composite scores per state variable, each from a few well-understood inputs, and give those to the classifier. The classifier then has five to ten inputs, which its episode count can support.

3.14 A data map

The table lists free sources and the depth of their daily history, which sets how many episodes a classifier can learn from.

Input State variable Free source Daily history from Published Revised
US market total return quantity of risk, direction Kenneth French data library 1926 monthly batches rarely
VIX quantity of risk Cboe 1990 same day no
VIX9D, VIX3M, VIX6M term structure Cboe 2011, 2009, 2008 same day no
VVIX, SKEW volatility of volatility, tails Cboe 2006, 1990 same day no
COR1M, COR3M implied correlation Cboe 2006 same day no
MOVE rates volatility ICE, via data vendors 1988 same day no
Baa minus 10-year credit FRED 1986 next day no
High-yield and investment-grade OAS credit FRED (three-year window) rolling next day no

10y–3m and 10y–2y spreads macro, policy FRED 1982, 1976 next day no
