Two gaps recur. Long, free histories of high-yield spreads no longer exist on FRED, so a study that needs them must store its own copy or use the Baa spread and the excess bond premium. And the volatility term structure, implied correlation and most cross-asset volatility indices start between 2006 and 2011, so a model that uses them has seen only two or three stress episodes. Several of those indices were also launched years after the start of their published history, and the earlier values are back-calculations from archived option prices: point-in-time in their inputs, but never published at the time.

§3 Key takeaways

  1. Choose inputs by the state variable the label depends on. For risk labels that means volatility inputs first; for macro labels, the curve and credit.
  2. The price path is the first input, not the last. It has the longest history, is never revised, and in the worked example no other input set beat it by more than 0.01 of AUC.
  3. The VIX is the best single forward-looking volatility input. The term structure, implied correlation and cross-asset volatility indices add little on average and have short histories.
  4. Credit can lead equity in credit-led stress, as in 2007. It is the main reason to include a second factor.
  5. Public sentiment measures, including put/call ratios, are mostly a reflection of past returns, and their levels have structural breaks. Residualise them or leave them out.
  6. Align every input to its publication time, store vintages, forward-fill from release dates, and never normalise with full-sample statistics.
  7. Rolling z-scores measure surprise, not level. Use expanding percentiles for inputs whose level matters.
  8. The input space has about two dimensions: a fast volatility factor and a slow credit-and-curve factor. Five to ten well-chosen inputs are enough.

4. Labels: where the training targets come from

A supervised regime classifier is only as good as the label it is trained to predict, and the label is the part of a regime study that receives the least thought. This section treats labels as objects with measurable properties. It starts from one decomposition, surveys six sources of labels with a fixed set of fields, and ends with a checklist for vetting a label and a procedure for building training and test sets that never use a label before it was knowable.

4.1 The label master form

Every label is a rule applied to a window of data around its date:

\[ y_t = L\big(\underbrace{S_{t-a}, \dots, S_t}_{\text{past part: in } \mathcal{F}_t},\; \underbrace{S_{t+1}, \dots, S_{t+b}}_{\text{future part}}\big). \]

The past part is observable when the decision is made; the future part is not. Three properties of every label follow from its reach \(b\), and they are the first things to compute about a new label:

  1. The purge. At a refit date \(\tau\), the labels of the last \(b\) days before \(\tau\) are not yet known. Training on them uses information from after \(\tau\).
  2. The detection floor. A classifier can know the future part only by forecasting it. For labels whose future part is direction, that forecast is weak, so detection lags by roughly the reach.
  3. Censoring. The last \(b\) days of any sample have no label, or a provisional one. In a live system this is the present, where the labels are always missing.

A label is a proxy for an outcome that a decision cares about. It is a good label if it separates that outcome, if it persists over the decision’s horizon, if it does not change much when its parameters change slightly, if it has enough episodes to learn from, and if its reach leaves something to learn. §4.9 turns these into tests.

The six sources below are described with the same fields: the idea, the definition, the reach, the parameters, the episodes and persistence it typically produces, its stability, its decision relevance, its failure modes, and when to use it.

4.2 Contemporaneous rules

Idea. Label a day by a condition on data observed that day.

Definition. “The VIX closed above 30”; “the market closed at least 10% below its high”; “the NFCI is above zero”; “the price is below its 200-day average”; “trailing 21-day realised volatility is in the top fifth of its history”.

Reach. Zero. The label is in \(\mathcal{F}_t\).

Parameters. A threshold, sometimes a window.

Episodes and persistence. Many, and often too many: a contemporaneous rule flickers when its input hovers near the threshold. In the worked example the rule “10% below the high” produced 132 episodes since 1930 with a median length of three days (§6.2). Hysteresis, with separate thresholds for entering and leaving, removes most of the flicker (§5.2).

Stability. Usually moderate; the threshold matters.

Decision relevance. Direct when the decision itself is defined by the condition, as with a risk limit that binds when the VIX exceeds 30.

Failure modes. Training a model to predict a label with zero reach learns nothing that the rule does not already compute. Two supervised uses remain legitimate. The first is nowcasting a late-published rule: estimate this week’s NFCI from daily market data before Wednesday, or the monthly Sahm indicator from weekly claims. The second is forecasting the rule \(h\) days ahead, which turns it into a forward-outcome label (§4.5).

When to use it. As a regime when the decision needs only the current state; as a feature; and as a baseline for everything else.

4.3 Official and expert dating

Idea. Use the turning points published by an authority.

Definition. NBER business-cycle peaks and troughs; the OECD’s turning points in its composite leading indicators; crisis chronologies; the bear-market dates reported by the financial press.

Reach. Long and variable: the announcement lag. The NBER announced peaks an average of 7.3 months after they occurred and troughs 15 months after, over the cycles since 1978. The longest wait was 21 months, for the trough of March 1991.

Parameters. None that the user controls; the committee’s judgement is the parameter.

Episodes and persistence. Very few and very persistent: 12 US recessions since 1948, each lasting months.

Stability. High: dates are rarely revised.

Decision relevance. High when a mandate or a contract keys off the official event; otherwise indirect.

Failure modes. The dates are set with hindsight. A classifier trained on them learns to recognise a whole recession, including its first months, which at the time looked like an ordinary slowdown. Used without the announcement lag, the label is a look-ahead, and a backtest that conditions on it reports a fantasy (section 1.5 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models).

When to use it. As a benchmark, and as a target only for slow macro decisions, lagged by the real announcement delay.

4.4 Turning-point rules on the price path

Idea. Date peaks and troughs from the price path itself, by rule.

Definition. The ±\(\delta\) rule of §2.4: a peak is confirmed when the price falls \(\delta\) below its running high, a trough when it rises \(\delta\) above its running low, and the label marks the days between a peak and the following trough. Variants include the Bry–Boschan and Pagan–Sossounov algorithms (§2.4), within the general framework for dating cycles from turning points of Harding and Pagan (2002), drawdown-based phases, directional-change event series, which record each reversal of a fixed size and so measure time in price moves rather than days (Glattfelder, Dupuis & Olsen, 2011; Tsang, Tao, Serguieva & Ma, 2017), and the zigzag indicator of charting software [Practice].

Reach. Random: the confirmation lag. For the ±20% rule on the US market since 1926 the median lag was 70 trading days for bear markets (interquartile range 42–146) and 41 for bull markets (16–76). For ±15% the medians were 48 and 25 days.

An exact equivalence makes the structure plain. The rule’s real-time version is a hysteresis rule on drawdown and run-up. The ex-post label is that rule’s state with each switch moved back to the extreme that preceded it. The two labels differ only on the days between each turning point and its confirmation, which in the worked example are 20% of all days since 1927.

Two-sided smoothers used to define trends or cycles, such as centred moving averages, the Hodrick–Prescott filter and band-pass filters, have the same look-ahead in continuous form. The smoothed value at \(t\) depends on data after \(t\), and the values near the end of the sample are revised as data arrive (Hamilton, 2018).

Parameters. The threshold \(\delta\), or the window and minimum durations of a dating algorithm.

Episodes and persistence. Few and persistent: 31 bear markets at ±20% since 1926, 47 at ±15%, nine at ±20% since 2000.

Stability. High agreement, unstable counts. The ±20% and ±15% labels agree with \(\kappa = 0.88\), but the second has half again as many episodes and shorter confirmation lags.

Decision relevance. High for exposure decisions in principle. In practice the valuable part of the label is the unknowable part (§6.3).

Failure modes. Borderline episodes flip with the index and the threshold (§2.4). Bear-market rallies become bull markets. The final phase is censored: on any date, the labels after the most recent running extreme are unknown, and training on them leaks. The label rewards forecasting turning points, which is forecasting direction.

When to use it. For describing history and for benchmarking. As a training target only with the purge of §4.10 applied, and with the expectation that the classifier will mostly learn to read the drawdown. The literature comparing the two ways of defining bull and bear markets reaches a consistent split: rule-based dating describes them better in sample, and Markov-switching models forecast them better (Kole & van Dijk, 2017); using several markets’ returns jointly helps both (Liu, Maheu & Song, 2024).

4.5 Forward-outcome labels

Idea. Define the regime by what happens over a fixed window after \(t\), chosen to match the decision.

Definition. Several forms are common.

  • Forward volatility quantile. \(y_t = 1\) if realised volatility over \((t, t+h]\) exceeds \(q_t\), where \(q_t\) is a quantile of trailing \(h\)-day realised volatility over the history up to \(t\). With \(h = 21\) and the 80th percentile this is the “next month’s volatility in the top fifth” label of the worked example.
  • Forward drawdown event. \(y_t = 1\) if the largest fall within \((t, t+h]\), measured from \(S_t\) or any later peak in the window, exceeds a level such as 10%.
  • Forward return sign or quantile. \(y_t = 1\) if \(S_{t+h} < S_t\).
  • Triple barrier. Place an upper and a lower barrier, usually scaled by current volatility, and a time limit; the label records which is hit first (López de Prado, 2018).
  • Trend scanning. Fit linear trends over forward windows of several lengths and label by the sign of the slope with the largest \(t\)-statistic (López de Prado, 2020).

Reach. Fixed at \(h\), or bounded by the time limit.

Parameters. The horizon and the threshold. The threshold must be computed causally, with an expanding quantile rather than a quantile of the full sample, because a full-sample quantile carries information about the future into every label.

Episodes and persistence. Depends on what the future part measures. In the worked example the forward-volatility label had 166 episodes since 1930 (median length 16 days), the forward-drawdown label 71 (median 60 days), and the forward-return label 501, with a median length of four days: a direction label flickers because direction does not persist.

Stability. Good for volatility labels; poor for return labels.

Decision relevance. The highest of any source, because the label is the decision’s outcome by construction.

Failure modes.

  • Overlap. Consecutive labels share \(h - 1\) days of outcome, so neighbouring training rows are nearly copies of each other. Standard cross-validation, which scatters neighbours across folds, then measures memorisation. Purging (dropping the training rows whose label windows overlap the test block) and an embargo of at least \(h\) days (dropping the rows just after it) fix this (López de Prado, 2018; section 11 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models).
  • Full-sample thresholds, as above.
  • Horizon mismatch: a label with a one-month horizon trained for a decision held for a week.

When to use it. Whenever the decision can be written as a forward event. It is the default recommendation of this chapter.

4.6 Labels from a fitted model

Idea. Fit an unsupervised regime model to the history, and use its state sequence as the label.

Definition. The smoothed state probabilities of a hidden Markov model, computed by the backward smoother of Kim (1994), used as soft labels; the most likely state path; the state sequence of a statistical jump model, which minimises the distance of each day’s features from its state’s centroid plus a penalty \(\lambda\) for every switch (Bemporad, Breschi, Piga & Boyd, 2018; Nystrup, Lindström & Madsen, 2020; Aydınhan, Kolm, Mulvey & Shu, 2024); clusters from \(k\)-means or a Gaussian mixture (Botte & Bao, 2021), including clustering of whole return distributions with the Wasserstein distance (Horvath, Issa & Muguruza, 2024); and the segments of a change-point method.

Reach. Formally the whole sample, since a two-sided fit lets every observation influence every label. In practice the label of day \(t\) is settled by the data within a few persistence lengths of \(t\). The worked example measures it for a two-state jump model on exponentially weighted features with half-lives of 10 and 42 days and \(\lambda = 40\). The model’s forward-only state path, which uses no data after \(t\), agreed with its two-sided labels on 94% of days (\(\kappa = 0.84\)), and recognised entry into the high-risk state a median of eight trading days late (interquartile range 6–11). That is a reach of about a week and a half, against months for the ±20% rule.

A second leak sits in the parameters. A model fitted to the whole sample defines its states using data from after \(t\), even when its state assignment is causal. Refit the labelling model on data up to each refit date.

Parameters. The number of states, the features, and the persistence penalty or transition prior. The penalty sets the episode count directly: \(\lambda\) of 10, 40 and 100 gave 112, 54 and 29 high-risk episodes on the century of data, with median lengths of 30, 68 and 132 trading days.

Episodes and persistence. Chosen through the penalty.

Stability. Moderate. Labels near the end of a fitting window are revised as data arrive, and states can swap identities between refits; identify each state by a fixed property, such as having the lower mean return or the higher volatility.

Decision relevance. Indirect. The model decides what a regime is, and a likelihood or a clustering objective usually decides it is volatility. That suits risk decisions and not much else.

Failure modes. The two leaks above; a definition chosen by the fitting objective rather than by the decision; and the false comfort of persistent labels, which make a classifier’s accuracy look high because yesterday’s label predicts today’s.

When to use it. When no decision-defined label exists and a persistent summary of many features is wanted, and as the teacher in a teacher–student pipeline (§5.8).

4.7 Strategy-outcome labels

Idea. Label a day by which of several actions would have done best after it.

Definition. Which of a set of strategies earned the highest risk-adjusted return over \((t, t+h]\); whether a base strategy’s trade opened at \(t\) made money, the meta-label of López de Prado (2018); whether a risky asset beat a haven over the next month.

Reach. \(h\).

Parameters. The set of strategies, the horizon, and the scoring rule.

Episodes and persistence. As noisy as the return differences they compare.

Stability. Low when strategies’ returns are close.

Decision relevance. Maximal for strategy selection: the label is the decision.

Failure modes. A strategy-outcome label is a direction label in disguise, because it depends on future returns. Choosing among many strategies inflates the apparent skill of the selector, and the comparison must be made net of costs.

When to use it. When the regime study exists to switch between strategies. The meta-label is the better-behaved form: it asks only whether to act on a signal you already have, which is a narrower question than which strategy is best.

4.8 Comparison of label sources

The fields that discriminate, in one table. The learnability ratings are this chapter’s assessment, informed by the worked example.

Source Reach What a classifier can learn Typical US episodes Persistence Main failure
Contemporaneous rule 0 nothing: compute it many low without hysteresis flicker
Official dating months to years slow macro forecasts 12 recessions since 1948 very high used without the announcement lag
Turning-point rule random, median 70 days at bear onsets mostly the current drawdown 31 bears since 1926 high the value lies in the unknowable days
Forward outcome, volatility \(h\) a great deal (AUC near 0.88) over a hundred moderate overlap ignored in validation
Forward outcome, drawdown \(h\) some (AUC near 0.65) dozens moderate overlap; few severe events
Forward outcome, return \(h\) almost nothing (AUC near 0.45) hundreds of flickers very low mistaken for a regime
Fitted model whole sample, about eight days in practice the model’s volatility state set by the penalty high two-sided labels, full-sample parameters
Strategy outcome \(h\) as much as the return gap allows depends low a direction label in disguise

4.9 Vetting a label before training anything

Five checks, each with a number to compute. A label that fails one of them will not be rescued by a better model.

  1. Decision relevance. Compare the outcome the decision cares about across the label’s classes: the strategy’s forward Sharpe ratio, the forward volatility, the forward drawdown. If the classes do not separate it, the label is the wrong label. A volatility label that separates forward volatility but not the strategy’s returns serves a sizing decision and not a timing one.
  2. Episodes and persistence. Count the episodes and their median length. The median length should exceed the decision’s holding period, and the episodes should number at least a few dozen in the training set. Fewer than about twenty training episodes leaves too little to learn from [Practice]; the test period needs its own episodes as well (§4.10).
  3. Stability. Recompute the label with its parameters moved by a fifth to a half (the threshold from 20% to 15%, the horizon from 21 to 15 or 30 days) and measure Cohen’s kappa against the original. Kappa below about 0.7 means the label is mostly its parameters [Practice].
  4. Reach and censoring. Compute the reach: fixed, or the distribution of confirmation lags. It sets the purge, the embargo and the expected detection lag.
  5. The value of knowing it, and when. Compute what the decision would earn with the label known one day ahead (the oracle) and with the label known when it becomes known (the stale label). The oracle is the ceiling; the stale label is the floor any classifier must clear; the gap is what a classifier is for. For the ±20% bull–bear label the ceiling was a Sharpe ratio of 1.54 and the floor 0.46, against 0.45 for doing nothing (§6.3). A classifier that recovers a fifth of that gap would be remarkable; one that recovers none is the usual result.

4.10 Building the training and test sets

The procedure below prevents the leaks specific to regime labels. Each step names the leak it closes.

  1. Point-in-time features. Align every input to its publication time and use stored vintages for revised series (§3.11). Closes: look-ahead in the inputs.
  2. Causal label parameters. Compute thresholds with expanding windows. The outcome of a forward label lies in the future by design; its threshold must not. Closes: look-ahead in the definition.
  3. Train only on labels final at the refit date. At refit date \(\tau\), include day \(t\) only if its label was settled by \(\tau\): \(t \le \tau - b\) for a fixed reach; \(t\) up to the current running extreme (the latest high in a bull phase, the latest low in a bear phase) for a turning-point label; for a model-derived label, refit the labelling model on data up to \(\tau\) and use only labels older than its effective reach. Closes: the purge.
  4. Walk forward. Refit on an expanding or rolling window at a fixed cadence (quarterly or yearly) and predict the next period. When data are too scarce for that, use purged \(k\)-fold cross-validation with an embargo of at least the reach. Closes: evaluation on the training period.
  5. Keep episodes whole. Never let one episode contribute rows to both the training and the test side of a split. With overlapping labels, a split in the middle of an episode puts nearly identical rows on both sides. Closes: memorisation scored as skill.
  6. Weight for overlap. Down-weight rows whose labels share outcomes, using the average uniqueness of each label (López de Prado, 2018), or keep every \(b\)-th row. This does not change the point estimates of a well-specified model much, but it stops the effective sample size from being overstated by a factor of \(b\).
  7. Leave class balance alone if you need probabilities. Oversampling the rare class distorts predicted probabilities. Use class weights only if the decision uses ranks rather than probabilities, and recalibrate afterwards.
  8. Size the test set by episodes. A test period should contain at least ten episodes of the minority class, and results should be reported per episode as well as per day.
  9. Prefer soft labels where they exist. Smoothed state probabilities carry the labelling model’s own uncertainty, and training against them, as in knowledge distillation (Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, 2015), wastes less information than training against their rounded values.
  10. Know where the label noise is. Classifiers tolerate label noise that is unrelated to the features (Frénay & Verleysen, 2014). Regime label noise is not of that kind: it concentrates at transitions, exactly where the features are changing. Expect a classifier to be least reliable at the moments that matter most.

§4 Key takeaways

  1. Every label is a rule on a window of data around its date. Compute its reach first: it sets the purge, the detection floor and the censoring.
  2. Contemporaneous rules have zero reach. Compute them; train a model on them only to nowcast a late-published value or to forecast the rule ahead.
  3. Official and expert dates are hindsight. Lag them by their real announcement delay or do not train on them.
  4. Turning-point labels are a real-time hysteresis rule with its switches back-dated. The back-dated days are a fifth of history and hold all of the label’s value.
  5. Forward-outcome labels are the default: they are the decision’s outcome by construction. Their thresholds must be causal and their overlap purged.
  6. Model-derived labels inherit two leaks: two-sided state assignment and full-sample parameters. Refit the labeller at every refit date.
  7. Vet a label before modelling it: decision relevance, episodes, stability, reach, and the gap between the oracle and the stale label.
  8. Train only on labels that were final at the refit date, keep episodes whole across splits, and size test sets by episodes.

5. Classifiers

With inputs chosen and a label vetted, the remaining choice is the model. It matters less than the two choices before it. In the worked example, going from a one-input to a twelve-input model added 0.04 of AUC on the volatility label (0.84 to 0.88), while moving from the volatility label to a direction label cost 0.44 (0.88 to 0.44), eleven times as much (§6.4). This section surveys the models with a fixed set of fields: the idea, the definition, the assumptions (and which are false in practice), strengths, weaknesses, cost, robustness, failure modes and when to reach for it. It begins with the baselines, because a classifier is only as good as its margin over them, and ends with the post-processing that turns a flickering probability into a usable regime.

5.1 The baselines every classifier must beat

Two baselines matter, and a classifier should be scored against both.

Climatology predicts the base rate of the label in the training data, the same probability every day. Its skill is zero by definition, and the Brier skill score (§7.1) measures improvement over it: \(\mathrm{BSS} = 1 - \mathrm{BS}_{\text{model}} / \mathrm{BS}_{\text{climatology}}\).

The stale label predicts the current label from the most recent label already known (§1.4): trailing realised volatility for a forward-volatility label, the confirmed state for a turning-point label. It captures persistence, and persistence is most of what any regime classifier exploits. In the worked example the stale label for next month’s volatility already had a Brier skill score of 0.34 and an AUC of 0.84 (§6.4).

Recommendation. Report skill over climatology for comparability with the literature, and skill over the stale label for the decision. A model that does not beat the stale label is a slow way to compute it.

5.2 Threshold rules with hysteresis

Idea. Switch regime when an observable crosses a threshold, with a gap between the entry and exit thresholds so the regime does not flicker.

Definition. For a single input \(x_t\) and thresholds \(u_{\text{out}} < u_{\text{in}}\):

\[ s_t = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x_t \ge u_{\text{in}}, \\ 0 & \text{if } x_t < u_{\text{out}}, \\ s_{t-1} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]

The regime enters at \(u_{\text{in}}\) and stays until the input falls below \(u_{\text{out}}\); with \(u_{\text{out}} = u_{\text{in}}\) the rule is a plain threshold and flickers. The real-time ±20% bull–bear rule is this rule with the watched input changing with the state: the drawdown from the running peak starts the bear state at 20%, and the run-up from the running trough ends it at 20%.

Assumptions. The regime is a monotone function of one observable. True for volatility regimes; false for most others.

Strengths. Transparent, with no estimation and no training labels; easy to monitor; hard to overfit.

Weaknesses. One input; fixed thresholds that age badly when the input’s level drifts (§2.3).

Cost. Negligible.

Robustness. High to noise, given hysteresis; low to level drift.

Failure modes. Thresholds set on the full sample leak; thresholds that are never revisited misclassify whole decades; without hysteresis, flicker.

When to reach for it. When the regime is the observable, as with “VIX above 30”, and as the baseline for every other model.

5.3 Composite indices

Idea. Combine several standardised inputs into one score, then threshold the score.

Definition. With \(\tilde x_{j,t}\) the causally standardised \(j\)-th input, signed so that a higher value means more of the state variable (more risk, more stress),

\[ I_t = \sum_{j=1}^{d} w_j\, \tilde x_{j,t}, \]

with weights \(w_j\) that are equal, taken from the first principal component, from a dynamic factor model (the NFCI), or from cross-correlations (the CISS). Turbulence is a quadratic cousin that uses the inverse covariance matrix: with \(R_t\) the vector of returns on \(m\) assets, and their mean \(\bar R\) and covariance \(\Sigma\) estimated from data up to \(t\), \(D_t = (R_t - \bar R)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (R_t - \bar R)\). This is the squared Mahalanobis distance of today’s returns from their mean: for one asset, the squared \(z\)-score; in general, large on days when assets move unusually far or in unusual combinations.

Assumptions. The inputs share one dominant factor and the factor is the state variable of interest. For volatility and stress this holds well (§3.13).

Strengths. Uses many inputs with few parameters; averages away input-specific noise; needs no labels.

Weaknesses. It summarises co-movement among the inputs, not the outcome a decision cares about, so its relationship to the label must still be checked.

Cost. Low.

Robustness. Equal weights are more robust than estimated ones when episodes are few [Practice].

Failure modes. Weights or normalisations estimated on the full sample; an input whose behaviour changes (the put/call ratio, §3.9) silently changing the index; rolling standardisation that turns the index into a surprise measure.

When to reach for it. To build the state scores of §3.13 that a classifier then uses, or as the regime itself when no label is available.

5.4 Logistic and probit models

Idea. Model the probability of the label as a smooth, monotone function of a weighted sum of inputs.

Definition. For a binary label,

\[ \Pr(y_t = 1 \mid x_t) = \Lambda\big(\beta_0 + \beta^\top x_t\big), \qquad \Lambda(u) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-u}}, \]

fitted by maximum likelihood with a ridge penalty: on standardised inputs, the coefficients minimise the negative log-likelihood summed over the \(n\) training rows plus \(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\alpha\, n \lVert \beta \rVert^2\), with the intercept \(\beta_0\) left unpenalised. Dividing by \(n\), this is the mean negative log-likelihood plus \(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\alpha \lVert \beta \rVert^2\), so \(\alpha\) means the same at any sample size. The penalty shrinks the coefficients towards zero: at \(\alpha = 0\) the fit is plain maximum likelihood, and as \(\alpha\) grows the model collapses to climatology (\(\beta = 0\), the base rate).

Three variants. The probit model replaces \(\Lambda\) with the normal distribution function and behaves almost identically. For ordered regimes (low, normal, high, crisis), the ordered logit uses one coefficient vector and \(K - 1\) increasing cut points \(\gamma_k\): \(\Pr(s_t \le k \mid x_t) = \Lambda(\gamma_k - \beta^\top x_t)\). Dynamic binary models add the lagged label or a lagged latent index to the right-hand side, and are the standard tools for recession and bear-market forecasting (Kauppi & Saikkonen, 2008; Nyberg, 2013; Chen, 2009).

Assumptions. The log-odds of the label are linear in the inputs. The assumption is false at the extremes, which is why inputs are logged, clipped and standardised first.

Strengths. Calibrated probabilities when the model is roughly right; few parameters, so it is stable with few episodes; coefficients a human can read.

Weaknesses. No interactions unless added by hand; monotone in each input.

Cost. Negligible.

Robustness. Good with shrinkage, poor without it. In the worked example, with a penalty of \(\alpha = 0.001\) per training row, the twelve-input model scored an AUC of 0.51 on the drawdown label, against 0.66 for a one-input model fitted the same way; with \(\alpha = 0.1\) it scored 0.64. Shrinkage matters because the effective sample is the number of episodes, not of rows.

Failure modes. In a dynamic model, a lagged label used without lagging it by its reach and publication delay: a lagged NBER indicator is not known at \(t - 1\). Extrapolation: a linear model meeting an input outside its training range produces extreme probabilities.

When to reach for it. By default. Recommendation: start every supervised regime study with a regularised logistic model on five to ten transformed inputs, and require any more complex model to beat it out of sample.

5.5 Tree ensembles

Idea. Combine many decision trees, each splitting the input space at thresholds, to capture non-linear effects and interactions.

Definition. Random forests average deep trees fitted to bootstrap samples; gradient boosting fits shallow trees in sequence, each to the errors of the ensemble so far.

Assumptions. Enough examples near each split to estimate it. With regime labels, “examples” means episodes.

Strengths. Interactions such as “high volatility and a downtrend” without specifying them; insensitivity to monotone transforms of the inputs; tolerance of uninformative inputs (Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux, 2022).

Weaknesses. More parameters to fit from the same few episodes; predicted probabilities that need recalibration; and no extrapolation. A tree treats a VIX of 80 like the highest VIX in its training data.

Cost. Moderate; trivial at daily frequency.

Robustness. Sensitive to the depth, the learning rate and the number of trees; tune them with purged validation.

Failure modes. Overfitting to a handful of crises that dominate the high-volatility region of the input space; a stepwise response that flips the regime at an arbitrary split.

When to reach for it. For labels with a hundred or more episodes, such as volatility labels, and for heterogeneous inputs. It is the classifier of the best-known teacher–student study (§5.8).

5.6 Sequence models

Idea. Let a recurrent or attention-based network learn its own features from the raw history of the inputs.

Definition. Recurrent networks, temporal convolutional networks and transformers mapping a window of past inputs to label probabilities.

Assumptions. Enough data to learn features that hand-made ones miss.

Strengths. No feature engineering; can find temporal patterns.

Weaknesses. Data-hungry, with a few dozen episodes to learn from; opaque; unstable across training runs.

Cost. High.

Robustness. Low with small samples.

Failure modes. Memorising the few crises in the training data; leakage through normalisation layers fitted on the full sample.

When to reach for it. Rarely, for regime labels. The most convincing use of learned macroeconomic states is inside a larger asset-pricing objective rather than as a standalone regime classifier (Chen, Pelger & Zhu, 2024). A network that does not beat a regularised logistic model with good inputs is the expected outcome [Practice].

5.7 Latent-state models with observable drivers

Idea. Skip the labels: let a hidden Markov model or Markov-switching model infer the regime from the inputs, with persistence built in.

Definition. A hidden Markov model whose emissions are the multivariate inputs; a Markov-switching model whose transition probabilities depend on observables (Diebold, Lee & Weinbach, 1994; Filardo, 1994); a Markov-switching dynamic factor model of economic activity (Chauvet & Piger, 2008). The companion chapter covers estimation in detail (section 5 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models).

Assumptions. A small number of states with constant emission distributions and Markov persistence.

Strengths. Probabilities and persistence come with the model; no labels to construct; a predictive density.

Weaknesses. The fitted states mean whatever the likelihood prefers, usually volatility; transition probabilities are estimated from the few transitions in the sample.

Cost. Moderate.

Robustness. Improved by heavy-tailed emissions and persistence priors (section 6 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models).

Failure modes. Smoothed probabilities used as real-time signals; states that change meaning between refits.

When to reach for it. When no external label suits the decision and a probabilistic, persistent state is wanted. Its filter is also the post-processor of §5.11, where it smooths another model’s output.

5.8 Teacher–student pipelines

Idea. Use an unsupervised model to define the regimes (the teacher), then train a supervised classifier on causal inputs to predict them (the student).

Definition. Fit a statistical jump model or hidden Markov model to features of past returns. Its two-sided state sequence becomes the label. Train a classifier, often gradient boosting, on inputs known at \(t\), including cross-asset and macroeconomic data the teacher never saw. Shu, Yu and Mulvey (2024b) label bullish and bearish regimes for each of twelve assets with jump models, forecast them with gradient-boosted trees using asset-specific and cross-asset macro features, and report better portfolios across several allocation methods from 1991 to 2023 [Contested]: one study, by the method’s developers, and at odds with the small gains from cross-asset inputs in the worked example (§6.4). The same group uses jump-model regimes for downside-risk reduction (Shu, Yu & Mulvey, 2024a) and for factor allocation (Shu & Mulvey, 2024). Earlier studies used the same design with other teachers. Hauptmann, Hoppenkamps, Min, Ramsauer and Zagst (2014) forecast the filtered probabilities of a two-regime Markov-switching model of monthly S&P 500 returns with logistic regressions. Uysal and Mulvey (2021) estimate the probability of a recession or a stock-market contraction with random forests on a large macroeconomic database, out of sample from 1973.

Assumptions. The teacher’s regimes matter for the decision, and the student’s inputs carry information about the teacher’s labels beyond what the teacher’s own causal state already has.

Strengths. Persistent labels with no external definition; access to the full supervised toolbox; the student can use inputs the teacher could not model.

Weaknesses. Two leaks inherited from model-derived labels (§4.6): two-sided state assignment and full-sample parameters. The student learns to predict the teacher, not the outcome; if the teacher’s states are volatility states, the student is a volatility forecaster with extra steps.

Cost. Moderate.

Robustness. Depends on the teacher’s stability across refits.

Failure modes. A student scored against labels from a teacher fitted on the whole sample, which overstates its accuracy near transitions. Labels near each refit date that the next refit revises.

When to reach for it. When a persistent regime definition is wanted and labels must come from somewhere. The procedure: refit the teacher at each refit date on data up to that date; train the student only on labels older than the teacher’s effective reach; score the student against the teacher’s own causal state as the stale-label baseline. The method is a form of knowledge distillation (Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, 2015), and training against the teacher’s soft probabilities rather than its hard states keeps the teacher’s uncertainty.

5.9 Change-point alarms

Idea. Detect that the data-generating process has changed, without saying which of \(K\) known regimes it changed to.

Definition. Cumulative-sum (CUSUM) detectors accumulate evidence of a shift in mean or variance and alarm at a threshold. Bayesian online change-point detection maintains a posterior over the time since the last change, the run length, updated with each observation (Adams & MacKay, 2007).

Assumptions. Segments are internally stable and changes are abrupt.

Strengths. Answers “did something just change?”, which is often the operative question; explicit control of false alarms; no labels.

Weaknesses. Says nothing about what the new state is; non-recurrent by design.

Cost. Low to moderate.

Robustness. Sensitive to the assumed size of the change and to the prior on run length.

Failure modes. Alarms on every volatility burst in fat-tailed data unless the observation model has heavy tails.

When to reach for it. As a monitoring layer beside a classifier: an alarm that the inputs’ behaviour has shifted, prompting review or a reduction in size.

5.10 Skipping the regime

Idea. Forecast the quantity the decision needs directly, and discretise only for communication, if at all.

Definition. For a sizing decision, forecast next month’s volatility with a regression on trailing realised volatility at daily, weekly and monthly scales (Corsi, 2009) and on the VIX, and size inversely to the forecast. For a drawdown decision, forecast a low quantile of next quarter’s return with quantile regression on stress inputs, as growth-at-risk does for GDP (Adrian, Boyarchenko & Giannone, 2019).

Assumptions. The decision is a smooth function of the forecast.

Strengths. No information is thrown away by coarsening; no label construction; the forecast can be evaluated directly.

Weaknesses. Less interpretable than a named regime; discrete decisions still need a threshold somewhere.

Cost. Low.

Robustness. High.

Failure modes. The same input-timing leaks as everything else.

When to reach for it. First. Recommendation: build the continuous forecast before the regime classifier, and adopt a discrete regime only where it improves the decision over the forecast it coarsens. The companion chapter reaches the same conclusion from the latent-state side: size continuously, do not gate (section 12 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models).

5.11 Post-processing: calibration, smoothing and hysteresis

A classifier’s daily probability is noisy, and a regime should not change every time it crosses one half. Four post-processing steps, in increasing order of structure:

  1. Calibration. Map raw scores to probabilities that match observed frequencies, by fitting a logistic curve to the scores (Platt scaling) or a monotone step function (isotonic regression). Fit it on training-period data only, and for a flexible model on out-of-fold scores, because such a model’s scores on its own training rows are too confident. Tree ensembles need it most (Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana, 2005).

  2. Smoothing. An exponentially weighted average of the probability trades a few days of delay for stability.

  3. Hysteresis. Enter the regime when the probability exceeds, say, 0.6, and leave when it falls below 0.4 (§5.2).

  4. A Markov filter over the classifier. Treat the classifier’s output as evidence and run it through a persistent Markov chain. With \(\pi_k\) the share of class \(k\) in the classifier’s training data and \(p_{jk}\) the probability of moving from class \(j\) to class \(k\) in a day, the filtered belief \(\tilde\xi_t\) updates as

    \[ \tilde\xi_t^{(k)} \;\propto\; \Big(\sum_{j} p_{jk}\, \tilde\xi_{t-1}^{(j)}\Big)\, \frac{\hat p_t^{(k)}}{\pi_k}. \]

    The ratio \(\hat p_t^{(k)} / \pi_k\) is the classifier’s evidence for class \(k\), with its training prior divided out; the sum carries yesterday’s belief forward through the chain. This is the Hamilton filter (section 5 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models) with the classifier in the place of the emission density, and it is how speech recognition combined neural networks with hidden Markov models (Bourlard & Morgan, 1994). The stickiness of \(p_{jk}\) sets the trade between delay and flicker: with no persistence (\(p_{jk} = \pi_k\) for every \(j\)) the filter returns the classifier’s own probability, and the stickier the chain, the more consecutive evidence it takes to move the belief. The filter treats each day’s evidence as independent given the state, which features built from overlapping windows are not, so read its output as a smoothed score rather than a calibrated probability.

For more than two ordered classes, smooth the cumulative probabilities rather than each class separately, so that the classes remain ordered.

5.12 Comparison

The ratings are this chapter’s assessment.

Method Needs labels Output Persistence Episodes needed Main failure Reach for it when
Threshold with hysteresis no state via hysteresis none level drift the regime is the observable
Composite index no score via smoothing none full-sample weights building state scores
Logistic or probit yes probability via inputs or a filter dozens extrapolation; unpurged lags the default supervised model
Tree ensemble yes score via a filter a hundred or more few episodes per split many episodes, many inputs
Sequence network yes probability learned many hundreds memorising crises seldom
Latent-state model no probability Markov dozens of transitions states mean volatility no external label fits
Teacher–student from a model probability from the teacher as the student needs two leaks from the teacher a persistent definition is wanted
Change-point alarm no run length by construction none fat-tail false alarms monitoring
Direct forecast no quantity via inputs none input leaks first, always

§5 Key takeaways

  1. Judge every classifier against the stale label as well as against the base rate. Persistence is most of what any regime classifier exploits.
  2. Start with a regularised logistic model on five to ten transformed inputs. Shrinkage matters because the effective sample is the number of episodes.
  3. Tree ensembles earn their complexity only on labels with a hundred or more episodes. Sequence networks rarely do.
  4. Composite indices are the right way to use many inputs: as a few state scores feeding a small classifier.
  5. Teacher–student pipelines inherit their teacher’s leaks. Refit the teacher at each refit date and score the student against the teacher’s causal state.
  6. Forecast the decision variable directly before building a regime, and keep the regime only if it improves the decision.
  7. Post-process probabilities: calibrate, then smooth with hysteresis or a Markov filter whose stickiness sets the trade between delay and flicker.

6. A worked example on a century of data

This section runs the chapter’s argument on public data. It builds eight definitions of a “bad” regime on a century of US stock returns, measures how much they agree, prices the hindsight in the most popular one, and then trains causal classifiers with and without cross-asset inputs to see what each kind of label allows them to learn. Every number is printed by figures/rc_common.py; the figures are drawn by figures/rc_labels.py and figures/rc_classifier.py.

6.1 Data and protocol

Data. The price path is the daily total return of the value-weighted US stock market from the Kenneth French data library, July 1926 to December 2025, 26,151 trading days. Until 1952 the library includes Saturday sessions, so the early years have up to about 300 trading days a year, and a 252-day “year” is shorter there. The VIX (from 1990) and the VIX3M (from September 2009) come from Cboe’s public history files. The Baa–Treasury spread (BAA10Y, from 1986), the 10-year minus 3-month Treasury spread (T10Y3M, from 1982) and the NBER recession indicator (USREC) come from FRED. The two FRED spreads are lagged one day, to their publication.

Labels. Nine labels, each marking a “bad” class: eight definitions and the ±15% variant of the first.

  1. Bear, ±20% rule, ex post: days from a peak to the following trough, where peaks and troughs are confirmed by 20% moves (§4.4).
  2. Bear, ±20% rule, as confirmed: the same rule’s real-time state.
  3. Bear, ±15% rule, ex post: as the first, with 15% thresholds.
  4. 10% below the high, now: the market closed at least 10% below its all-time high.
  5. Next-month volatility, top fifth: realised volatility over the next 21 trading days at or above the 80th percentile of trailing 21-day realised volatility up to \(t\), an expanding threshold used after a burn-in of 1,260 trading days (five years at 252 a year).
  6. 10% drawdown in next quarter: a fall of at least 10% within the next 63 trading days.
  7. Negative next-quarter return: the market lower 63 trading days later.
  8. Jump model, high-risk state: the two-sided state sequence of a two-state statistical jump model with \(\lambda = 40\), fitted on the data from 1927 on. Its features are exponentially weighted means and downside deviations of daily returns, with half-lives of 10 and 42 days.
  9. NBER recession: months the NBER dates as recession, without any announcement lag; it is used here only to compare with the others.

Classifiers. Logistic regressions (§5.4) with a ridge penalty of \(\alpha = 0.1\) per training row on standardised inputs, refitted every January from 2000 to 2025. Each refit uses all rows since January 1990 whose label was final by the refit date: rows older than the label’s reach for forward labels, and rows up to the last confirmed extreme for the ex-post bear label. Four input sets are compared. Vol-only is the log of trailing 21-day realised volatility, the stale label for the volatility target. VIX-only is the log VIX. Price has seven price-path features: log realised volatility over 5, 21 and 63 days, the drawdown from the one-year high, the 12-month and 1-month log returns, and the log distance from the 200-day average. Price + cross-asset, the full model, adds five more: the log VIX, a variance-risk-premium proxy (the log VIX minus log realised volatility), the Baa spread, its 21-day change, and the 10-year minus 3-month spread.

Scores. AUC and the Brier skill score (§5.1, §7.1, §7.3) against climatology, the base rate in each refit’s training data, on the 2000–2025 test predictions. An AUC of 0.5 is chance, and a Brier skill of 0 is no better than climatology. Differences between models come with 90% intervals from a bootstrap that resamples one-year blocks of the test period.

6.2 Eight definitions, one century: how much they agree

The labels are compared on the days where all of them are defined, October 1930 to October 2025 (24,809 days). The start is set by the 1,260-day burn-in of the volatility threshold, the end by the 63-day forward windows. The ±20% rule finds 31 bear markets since 1926; the first ends before the common sample begins, so the table counts 30. For the same reason it counts 45 of the 47 bear markets of the ±15% rule.

Label Share of days in the bad class Episodes Median length (days) Reach
Bear, ±20% rule, ex post 19% 30 128 confirmation lag, median 70 at bear onsets
Bear, ±20% rule, as confirmed 14% 30 93 0
Bear, ±15% rule, ex post 20% 45 71 confirmation lag, median 48 at bear onsets
10% below the high, now 40% 132 3 0

10% drawdown in next quarter 21% 71 60 63 days
Negative next-quarter return 32% 501 4 63 days

NBER recession 16% 15 209 months to years

The next table gives Cohen’s kappa for each pair of labels, on the same days. Kappa corrects the raw share of agreement for the agreement that two labels with these base rates would reach by chance (Cohen, 1960):

\[ \kappa = \frac{\text{agreement observed} - \text{agreement by chance}}{1 - \text{agreement by chance}}. \]

Two labels with base rates \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\) agree by chance on a share \(\pi_A \pi_B + (1 - \pi_A)(1 - \pi_B)\) of days. A kappa of 1 is perfect agreement and 0 is no better than chance.
