Four readings:

  1. Definitions in different families agree only moderately. Apart from the ±20% and ±15% versions of the ex-post bear label, no pair reaches 0.6. There is no single regime history that all reasonable definitions recover.
  2. Thresholds matter less than hindsight. The ±20% and ±15% ex-post labels agree at 0.88. The ±20% ex-post label and its own real-time version agree at 0.27.
  3. The ex-post bear label is mostly about the future. It agrees better with future outcomes than with any rule that uses only the past: 0.58 with a 10% drawdown in the next quarter, 0.38 with a negative next quarter and 0.35 with high volatility next month, against 0.27 with its own real-time version and 0.33 with 10% below the high. The real-time version agrees with a negative next quarter at 0.03, which is to say not at all.
  4. The jump model sits in the middle. It agrees with almost everything at about 0.5 and with the direction label at 0.11, as a volatility state should.

Figure 1 shows eight of them, all but the ±15% variant, from 1995 to 2025.

Figure 1. Eight definitions of a bad regime, 1995–2025. Rust strips are rules on the price path, teal strips outcomes over the next month or quarter, gold strips a fitted model and the NBER. Grey at the right edge marks the final weeks, where forward labels are not yet defined.

6.3 The price of hindsight: the ±20% rule

The ±20% rule is the most widely quoted regime definition, and its real-time version can be compared with its ex-post version exactly.

Confirmation lags. Since 1926, a bear market was confirmed a median of 70 trading days after its peak (interquartile range 42–146), and a bull market a median of 41 trading days after its trough (16–76). With 15% thresholds the medians fall to 48 and 25. On 20% of all days since 1927, the confirmed state and the ex-post label disagree: on 12.7% of days the label is bear while the confirmed state still says bull, and on 7.4% the reverse.

The bear markets since 2000 show the range:

Peak Confirmed Trading days to confirmation Fall at confirmation
24 Mar 2000 20 Dec 2000 188 21.9%
21 May 2001 17 Sep 2001 78 21.1%
19 Mar 2002 10 Jul 2002 78 20.2%
9 Oct 2007 15 Jul 2008 192 20.3%
6 Jan 2009 27 Feb 2009 36 20.4%
29 Apr 2011 3 Oct 2011 108 20.3%
20 Sep 2018 24 Dec 2018 65 20.4%
19 Feb 2020 12 Mar 2020 16 27.5%
8 Nov 2021 19 May 2022 133 20.0%

In 2011 and 2018 the bear market was confirmed on the day of its trough: the rule recognised the bear market on the day it ended. The 2020 bear market fell 27.5% in the sixteen days the rule needed.

What the label is worth, and when. Three ways to hold the US market or cash (the risk-free rate) from 1927 to 2025. The Sharpe ratio is computed from daily returns in excess of the risk-free rate, and the maximum drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough fall in wealth:

Strategy Compound annual return Sharpe ratio Maximum drawdown
Buy and hold 9.7% 0.45 84.1%
Out of the market in ex-post bear markets (the oracle) 24.2% 1.54 19.6%
Out of the market when the rule has confirmed a bear market 8.7% 0.46 61.3%

The oracle needs to know on each day whether that day belongs to a bear market, which is known only after confirmation. Using the rule’s state from the previous day instead, as a real system must, leaves the Sharpe ratio where buy and hold had it. The real-time rule does reduce the worst drawdown, from 84% to 61%, because it exits the deepest bear markets after their first 20%. The difference between 1.54 and 0.46 is the value of the unknowable 20% of days. It is the entire prize that a bull–bear classifier competes for, and it can be captured only by forecasting falls of 20% before they have happened.

6.4 What a causal classifier learns

The classifiers are trained on four of the labels: next-month volatility, a 10% drawdown in the next quarter, a negative next-quarter return and the ex-post ±20% bear label. Their future parts differ: volatility for the first, volatility and direction for the second, direction for the third, and for the fourth the current drawdown plus the direction of the coming months. Their out-of-sample scores, 2000–2025, as AUC with the Brier skill score against climatology in brackets:

Target Base rate Vol-only VIX-only Price Price + cross-asset
Next-month volatility, top fifth 0.32 0.84 (+0.34) 0.87 (+0.38) 0.87 (+0.45) 0.88 (+0.47)
10% drawdown in next quarter 0.24 0.62 (+0.09) 0.61 (+0.08) 0.67 (+0.10) 0.64 (+0.07)
Negative next-quarter return 0.32 0.43 (−0.00) 0.39 (−0.00) 0.45 (−0.04) 0.44 (−0.08)
Bear, ±20% rule, ex post 0.19 0.71 (+0.15) 0.69 (+0.13) 0.83 (+0.27) 0.81 (+0.27)

The base rate is the share of test days in the bad class. For the volatility label it is 0.32, above the 17% of §6.2, because the threshold is an expanding quantile and the years since 2000 were more volatile than the history before them.

The 90% bootstrap intervals for the gain of the full model over the price-only model:

Target Gain in AUC Gain in Brier skill
Next-month volatility, top fifth [+0.001, +0.025] [−0.003, +0.039]
10% drawdown in next quarter [−0.085, −0.006] [−0.077, −0.003]
Negative next-quarter return [−0.042, +0.028] [−0.089, −0.007]
Bear, ±20% rule, ex post [−0.036, +0.002] [−0.030, +0.034]

Against the volatility-only model, the full model’s gain on the volatility target is [+0.023, +0.056] in AUC and [+0.10, +0.17] in Brier skill.

Five findings:

  1. Volatility labels are learnable, and mostly from persistence. Trailing realised volatility alone forecasts next month’s volatility regime with an AUC of 0.84. The VIX does better (0.87), as a forward-looking input should, and the full model adds about another 0.01.
  2. Direction labels are not learnable. Every input set scores below 0.5 on the negative-next-quarter label, and none beats climatology on the Brier score. An AUC below 0.5 means that the model’s riskier days were followed by a loss less often than its safer days. What the models learned about the link between volatility and the next quarter’s direction did not hold in the next period: 2009 and 2020 began their recoveries near the peak of measured risk.
  3. Drawdown labels sit in between, through volatility. A 10% drawdown is more likely when volatility is high, simply because a large fall is easier when the market moves more. The skill is real but small (Brier skill about 0.1), and the cross-asset inputs make it worse rather than better.
  4. The ex-post bear label is nowcastable, but only as far as the drawdown has already happened. Price features reach an AUC of 0.83. The model is largely reading the drawdown and the volatility that come with a bear market already under way (§6.5).
  5. The cross-asset inputs add almost nothing on these targets. The VIX, the variance risk premium, the credit spread and the yield curve improve the volatility forecast over trailing volatility alone. Over the seven price features they add at most 0.01 of AUC on the volatility target (a 90% interval of +0.001 to +0.025, with the Brier-skill interval straddling zero), and on the other targets they make no difference or hurt. Two further checks point the same way. Adding the VIX/VIX3M term-structure ratio to models trained from September 2009, and testing on 2015–2025, left the volatility AUC at 0.77 and lowered the bear-label AUC from 0.78 to 0.76. A model without the term-structure ratio but trained from 1990 scored 0.80 and 0.81 on the same test years. Nineteen more years of history were worth more than the extra input. And with weak shrinkage (\(\alpha = 0.001\)), the twelve-input model’s AUC on the drawdown label fell to 0.51, against 0.66 for the volatility-only model fitted the same way.

6.5 Detection at bear-market onsets

For the ex-post bear label, the question a practitioner asks is how soon after each peak the classifier says “bear”. The table counts trading days from each peak since 2000 to the rule’s confirmation, and to the first day the walk-forward classifier’s probability reached one half.

Peak Peak to trough (days) Rule confirms Price model Price + cross-asset
24 Mar 2000 259 188 15 15
21 May 2001 82 78 4 6
19 Mar 2002 142 78 36 68
9 Oct 2007 283 192 69 31
6 Jan 2009 42 36 1 1
29 Apr 2011 108 108 67 68
20 Sep 2018 65 65 62 55
19 Feb 2020 23 16 12 6
8 Nov 2021 235 133 117 85

The classifiers cross one half well before the rule in the long bear markets of 2000 and 2007 (by 120 to 170 days), by 10 to 50 days in 2002, 2011 and 2021–22, and only days before it in the fast ones of 2018 and 2020. The first crossing flatters the classifier, though. The crossings of one to six days in 2001 and 2009 are artefacts: the probability had not fallen far below one half during the rally before each peak. Over the whole test period the full model’s probability was above one half on 39% of ex-post bear days and on 6% of bull days, with 12 false alarms of five days or more; the confirmed state was on for 29% of bear days and 8% of bull days. The classifier is an earlier, noisier version of the rule.

Figure 2 shows why. The classifier’s bear probability rises and falls with its forecast of volatility. It cannot see a bear-market rally such as November 2008 to January 2009, which the ±20% rule calls a bull market, and it lingers after the troughs, for weeks after March 2009 and less so after October 2022, when volatility was still elevated but the new bull market had begun.

Figure 2. Walk-forward probabilities through the bear markets of 2007–09, 2020 and 2022. Shaded: ex-post ±20% bear markets. Black: the full model’s probability of the ex-post bear label. Teal: its probability that next month’s volatility lands in the top fifth. Dashed grey: the rule’s confirmed state.

6.6 What the example does and does not show

The example supports the chapter’s spine. Labels whose future part is volatility were forecast well, mostly from persistence; labels whose future part is direction were not forecast at all; the bull–bear label’s value sat entirely in the days it could not be known; and the many inputs collapsed to the information already in the price path.

It does not show that cross-asset inputs are useless. Four limits matter:

  1. One market and one kind of label. All the targets are about US equities. Labels about credit, about the stock–bond correlation, or about a multi-asset portfolio would give credit spreads and the curve a direct role, and the episodes of 2007 suggest credit can lead (§2.11).
  2. A linear model. Interactions, such as high volatility together with widening spreads, were not offered. A tree ensemble could find them, at the cost of the few-episode problem.
  3. A short cross-asset history. The cross-asset inputs enter in 1990, so the classifier’s first refit, in January 2000, had seen two bear markets. The term-structure ratio starts in September 2009, so the first refit that used it, in January 2015, had seen one.
  4. Nine bear onsets. Every statement about detection in §6.5 rests on nine episodes. The bootstrap intervals in §6.4 resample years, not episodes, and so understate the uncertainty about bear-market detection.

Within those limits, the practical reading is direct. Start a regime study with volatility labels and price-path inputs. Add the VIX. Add any other input only when a decision-specific label shows that it beats that baseline out of sample.

§6 Key takeaways

  1. Eight reasonable definitions of a bad regime agree only moderately; apart from the ±20% and ±15% versions of the ex-post bear label, no pair reaches a kappa of 0.6.
  2. The ±20% bull–bear label is worth a Sharpe ratio of 1.54 known in advance and 0.46 known when confirmed, against 0.45 for buy and hold. Its value lies in the 20% of days it cannot be known.
  3. Next month’s volatility regime is forecast with an AUC near 0.88; trailing volatility alone reaches 0.84.
  4. Next quarter’s direction is not forecast: every input set scored below 0.5 out of sample.
  5. A bear-market classifier reads the drawdown and the volatility already present. It is an earlier, noisier version of the confirmation rule.
  6. The VIX, credit spreads, the yield curve and the volatility term structure add at most 0.01 of AUC to price-path features for these equity labels; longer history was worth more than an extra input.

7. Evaluating a regime classifier

A regime classifier produces a daily probability that is then turned into actions. Its evaluation therefore has three layers: the probability (is it accurate and calibrated?), the events (does it catch regime changes in time, and how often does it cry wolf?), and the decision (does acting on it pay after costs?). Each layer needs its own metric and the same discipline about uncertainty, because the sample is a few dozen episodes however many days it spans. The companion chapter’s research protocol applies in full (section 11 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models); this section adds what is specific to classifiers.

7.1 Proper scores and skill

A proper scoring rule is one whose expected value is best when the forecast probability equals the true probability, so it cannot be gamed by shading forecasts toward 0 or 1 (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007). Two are standard. The Brier score is the mean squared error of the probability over the \(n\) scored days,

\[ \mathrm{BS} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \big(\hat p_t - y_t\big)^2, \]

(Brier, 1950). The log loss, \(-\frac{1}{n}\sum_t \big[y_t \log \hat p_t + (1 - y_t)\log(1 - \hat p_t)\big]\), punishes confident errors far more heavily. The Brier score is the better default for regime work, because a single confident miss in a crisis should count, but should not dominate.

Raw scores depend on the base rate, so report skill against a reference forecast:

\[ \mathrm{BSS} = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{BS}_{\text{model}}}{\mathrm{BS}_{\text{reference}}}. \]

A score of 0 means no better than the reference, 1 means perfect, and negative values mean worse. Use two references (§5.1): climatology, for comparison with other studies, and the stale label, for the decision. As reference points from §6.4, with the best input set for each label: the next-month volatility label reached a Brier skill of 0.47 over climatology, the drawdown label 0.10, and the direction label a negative skill.

7.2 Calibration

A probability is calibrated if, among the days on which it says 30%, the label turns out positive on about 30%. Check it with a reliability table: group forecasts into bins, and compare each bin’s average forecast with its observed frequency. The Brier score splits into three parts, reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty (Murphy, 1973). With the forecasts grouped into bins \(k\), bin \(k\) holding \(n_k\) days with mean forecast \(\bar f_k\) and observed frequency \(\bar y_k\), and with \(\bar y\) the base rate over all \(n\) days,

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{BS} &= \underbrace{\sum_k \tfrac{n_k}{n}\,(\bar f_k - \bar y_k)^2}_{\text{reliability}} - \underbrace{\sum_k \tfrac{n_k}{n}\,(\bar y_k - \bar y)^2}_{\text{resolution}} \\[4pt] &\quad + \underbrace{\bar y\,(1 - \bar y)}_{\text{uncertainty}}. \end{aligned} \]

The identity is exact when all the forecasts in a bin are the same number; for continuous forecasts a small within-bin remainder is left over. Reliability measures miscalibration and should be small. Resolution measures how far the bins’ observed frequencies depart from the base rate, that is, how well the forecasts separate good days from bad, and should be large. Uncertainty is the base rate’s own variance, which no model can change.

Calibrate on training data only (on out-of-fold scores for a flexible model, §5.11), refit the calibration with the model, and check calibration separately in calm and stressed periods: a model can be calibrated on average and badly miscalibrated in exactly the periods that matter.

7.3 Discrimination when the class is rare

The AUC is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, which plots the share of positive days flagged against the share of negative days flagged as the threshold moves. It equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive day receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative day. It ignores calibration entirely, since any monotone transformation of the scores leaves it unchanged, so it measures ranking and nothing else. For a rough sense of scale, suppose the scores of positive and negative days were normal with equal spread and means \(\Delta\) standard deviations apart. A positive score minus a negative score is then normal with mean \(\Delta\) and variance 2, so \(\mathrm{AUC} = \Phi(\Delta / \sqrt{2})\), with \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function. An AUC of 0.84 means \(\Delta\) is about 1.4, and an AUC of 0.6 means about 0.36.

When the class of interest is rare, as crisis regimes are, the AUC can look reassuring while most of the alarms are false. The precision–recall curve, which plots the share of alarms that are correct against the share of positives caught, is more informative in that case (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015). Report precision at the threshold the decision will actually use.

7.4 Event metrics: delay, false alarms and flicker

Scores averaged over days hide what a regime classifier is for: catching changes. Four event metrics, computed per episode:

  1. Detection delay. Days from the start of each positive episode to the first day the probability crosses the decision threshold. Report the median and the worst case, and compare them with the stale label’s delay. For the ex-post bear label in §6.5, the price-feature classifier’s delay ranged from 1 to 117 trading days (the shortest are crossings that never reset after the previous bear market, as in 2009), against 16 to 192 for the confirmation rule.
  2. False alarms. Runs of at least \(m\) days above the threshold while the label is negative, per year. Set \(m\) by the decision: a sizing rule may tolerate one-day blips that a strategy switch cannot.
  3. Missed episodes. Positive episodes never detected before they end.
  4. Flips per year. The number of regime changes the post-processed output makes. Each flip has a trading cost, and the companion chapter’s cube-root rule for hysteresis bands applies (section 12 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models).

Delay and false alarms trade against each other as the threshold moves. Plot the whole trade-off rather than one point on it. This is the event-level analogue of the receiver operating characteristic, and the literature on monitoring for changes in behaviour treats it the same way (Fawcett & Provost, 1999).

7.5 Economic evaluation

The final test is the decision itself: what does acting on the classifier earn, after costs, against two alternatives? The first is the stale-label rule, which needs no model. The second is the continuous forecast that the regime coarsens (§5.10), such as sizing inversely to forecast volatility without any regime. A regime classifier that beats neither is not worth its complexity. In the worked example the real-time ±20% rule, used for timing, earned what buy and hold earned (§6.3); the classifier’s own timing value would have to be measured the same way, with its false alarms paid for: map the probability to a position by a stated rule, apply it with a one-day lag, charge a cost for every change of position, and compare the Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown with those of the two alternatives.

7.6 Uncertainty: count episodes, not days

Three tools, in increasing order of strength:

  1. Block bootstrap. Resample blocks of the test period long enough to contain whole episodes, a year or more for bear markets, as in §6.4 or, with random block lengths, as in the stationary bootstrap (Politis & Romano, 1994). Intervals from day-level resampling are far too narrow.
  2. A persistence-preserving permutation test. Break the link between the features and the label while keeping each one’s persistence: circularly shift the label sequence against the features by random offsets of at least a year, refit, and score. The distribution of scores under this null shows how much skill persistence and overlap alone produce.
  3. A synthetic null. Simulate price paths from a model with no regimes, such as a GARCH process fitted to the same data, compute the same labels, and run the whole pipeline. Any “skill” it finds in direction labels is an artefact of the pipeline.

Count the trials. Every label definition, threshold, horizon and input set tried is a trial, and the best of many trials overstates skill (Bailey & López de Prado, 2014; Harvey, Liu & Zhu, 2016).

7.7 A protocol

  1. Write the decision, label, horizon and reach in one sentence (§1.2).
  2. Vet the label: decision relevance, episodes, stability, reach, and the oracle and stale-label values (§4.9).
  3. Build point-in-time inputs and a walk-forward training set that uses only labels final at each refit date (§4.10).
  4. Fit the stale-label baseline and a regularised logistic model before anything else (§5.1, §5.4).
  5. Score probabilities with the Brier score against climatology and against the stale label, check calibration, and report AUC with precision at the decision threshold (§7.1–§7.3).
  6. Score events: delay, false alarms, misses and flips, per episode (§7.4).
  7. Score the decision after costs against the stale-label rule and the continuous alternative (§7.5).
  8. Put intervals on every comparison with a block bootstrap, run the permutation and synthetic nulls, and count the trials (§7.6).

§7 Key takeaways

  1. Score probabilities with a proper rule, the Brier score by default, as skill over climatology and over the stale label.
  2. Check calibration in calm and stressed periods separately.
  3. AUC measures ranking only. For rare crisis classes, report precision at the threshold you will use.
  4. Score events, not just days: detection delay, false alarms, misses and flips, per episode.
  5. The decision test compares the classifier with the stale-label rule and with the continuous forecast it coarsens, after costs.
  6. Resample whole episodes, test against nulls that keep persistence, and count every label, threshold and input set tried.

8. Building a regime study

This section turns the chapter into an architecture. It is generic: it assumes a daily data store, a study framework that computes derived series from inputs, and consumers such as position sizing. Its main recommendation is to make the study produce continuous scores and calibrated probabilities, with discrete regimes derived from them, rather than a single regime label.

8.1 A reference architecture

The study has five layers. Data flow through them in one direction, and a monitoring layer watches the data, the classifiers and the outputs.

The data store holds every input with the time it became available and, for revised series, every vintage (§3.11). Studies read only what was available at each date.

The state scores are a handful of continuous, causally standardised composites, one or two per state variable (§3.13): for example, a quantity-of-risk score from realised volatility at several horizons and the VIX, and a price-of-risk score from credit spreads and the variance risk premium. They are useful outputs in their own right.

The regime models are of two kinds. Rules and composite indices need no labels and produce regimes with zero reach. Classifiers are trained, one per vetted label and horizon, and produce probabilities.

Post-processing calibrates the probabilities and smooths them into regimes (§5.11).

The outputs go to consumers, each of which uses the output that suits it: sizing uses the risk score or the volatility probability, a strategy switch uses a smoothed regime, a risk limit uses a rule.

8.2 What the study should output

For each date, a regime study should publish:

  1. The state scores, as continuous values.
  2. A calibrated probability for each label, tagged with the label’s definition and horizon. “P = 0.7” is meaningless without “that next month’s realised volatility exceeds its historical 80th percentile”.
  3. The stale label or confirmed state, so that consumers and monitors can see the baseline the model is supposed to beat.
  4. The discrete regime, derived from the probability by a stated rule, never as the only output.
  5. Data-quality flags: which inputs were stale, missing or filled.
  6. The model version and training window, so that any output can be reproduced.

A study that outputs only a regime label throws away the probability, the uncertainty and the reason, and its consumers cannot size by confidence.

8.3 A staged build with gates

The early stages are infrastructure, and skipping them is the usual reason regime studies fail in production. Each stage has a gate that must be passed before the next begins.

Stage Build Gate
0. Data Point-in-time store; publication lags; vintages for revised series An audit shows no input is used before its publication time
1. Scores and rules State scores; rule-based regimes with hysteresis; stale labels Scores and rules behave as expected in known episodes (2008, 2020, 2022)
2. Labels Candidate labels for the decision; the five vetting checks At least one label passes all five checks (§4.9)
3. Classifier Regularised logistic model on five to ten inputs, walk-forward Brier skill over the stale label, with a block-bootstrap interval above zero
4. Decision The decision rule using the calibrated probability Beats the stale-label rule and the continuous alternative after costs
5. Production Monitoring, retraining schedule, fallbacks Drift and staleness alarms tested by injecting stale data

Most studies should stop at stage 1 or 2. A set of well-built state scores and rules, with hysteresis, delivers most of what a regime study can deliver for risk decisions, and stage 3 is worth building only where a vetted label shows a gap that a model can close.

8.4 Failure modes in production

  • Stale or missing inputs. A source stops updating, or a holiday calendar differs between sources, and the study silently forward-fills an old value. Flag inputs older than their expected publication lag, and degrade to rules that do not use them.
  • Revisions and backfills. A vendor revises history, and the next retraining learns from data that were never available live. Store what was fetched, when it was fetched.
  • Structural breaks in an input. The composition of option volume changed the meaning of put/call ratios (§3.9); an index methodology change shifts a level. Monitor each input’s distribution against its own history.
  • Label drift. The base rate of a label changes, for example because an expanding threshold adapts only slowly: the volatility label of §6.2 marks 17% of days over the century but 32% of the days since 2000 (§6.4). Report the base rate in each training window.
  • Calibration decay. Probabilities that were calibrated in training drift. Recheck the reliability table every retraining.
  • Regimes that change meaning. A retrained latent-state model or jump model swaps or redefines its states. Identify states by a fixed property and alarm on large label revisions.
  • Crowding. Many funds cutting risk on the same VIX threshold may amplify the moves they respond to [Hypothesis]. Prefer continuous sizing to hard thresholds, which also reduces the study’s own trading.

§8 Key takeaways

  1. Build in layers: point-in-time data, continuous state scores, rules and classifiers, post-processing, outputs, with monitoring across all of them.
  2. Output scores and calibrated probabilities with their label definitions, the stale baseline, data-quality flags and versions. Never only a regime label.
  3. Pass the gates in order. Data integrity and well-behaved state scores come before any classifier.
  4. Most studies should stop at state scores and rules with hysteresis. Train a classifier only where a vetted label shows a gap a model can close.
  5. In production, the failures are stale inputs, revisions, structural breaks in inputs and decaying calibration. Monitor all four.

9. Synthesis

9.1 The framework in one paragraph

A regime is a coarse partition of a few continuous state variables, chosen to serve a decision: the quantity of risk, the price of risk, direction, the macroeconomic state and structure. Inputs are noisy measurements of those state variables, and most of them measure the quantity of risk. A label is a rule on a window of the price path, and its reach (how far into the future the window extends) decides everything else: the purge in training, the floor on detection delay, and how much a classifier can learn. A supervised regime classifier is a forecaster of its label’s future part. When that future part is volatility, which persists, the classifier learns a great deal, mostly from the stale label. When it is direction, which does not persist, the classifier learns almost nothing, and the label’s value sits in the days when it cannot be known. The sample is the number of episodes, so models must be small and evaluation must resample episodes.

Decision State variable Label Reach First inputs First model Baseline to beat
Sizing, risk limits quantity of risk forward volatility quantile 21 days realised volatility, VIX logistic, or a direct volatility forecast trailing volatility
Drawdown control quantity of risk, direction forward drawdown event 63 days realised volatility, drawdown, VIX logistic trailing volatility
Exposure timing direction ex-post bull–bear or forward return months price path none worth fitting confirmed state; buy and hold
Leverage, liquidity price of risk, structure stress index above a threshold 0, plus publication lag spreads, stress indices rule with hysteresis; nowcast of the index the last published value
Strategic allocation macro lagged recession or growth–inflation phase months curve, credit, claims, surprises monthly logistic or probit the last published phase
Diversification structure correlation regime 0 (estimated) rolling correlations, implied correlation rule with hysteresis rolling estimate
Strategy selection depends meta-label of the base strategy its holding period the strategy’s own state plus risk inputs logistic always on

9.2 Decision tree

Whichever branch applies, the same steps come first: write the decision as a sentence, vet the label (§4.9), build the stale-label baseline, align every input to its publication time, and count episodes rather than days.

9.3 Ten rules for someone starting today

  1. Write the decision, the label, the horizon and the reach in one sentence before loading any data.
  2. Prefer labels whose future part is volatility. They can be forecast; direction cannot.
  3. Compute the label’s reach and purge accordingly. A label with zero reach is a rule: compute it, do not learn it.
  4. Beat the stale label, not the base rate.
  5. Start with the price path and the VIX. Add any other input only when it beats that baseline out of sample on a decision-specific label.
  6. Align every input to its publication time and store vintages of revised series.
  7. Use expanding percentiles for levels; keep rolling z-scores for surprises.
  8. Use a regularised logistic model on five to ten inputs before anything more complex, and calibrate whatever you use.
  9. Output continuous scores and calibrated probabilities; derive regimes from them with hysteresis.
  10. Count episodes, not days: resample them, test against nulls that keep persistence, and count every trial.

9.4 What is known, and what is not

Established. Volatility is persistent and forecastable from its own history and from implied volatility, so regimes defined by future risk can be forecast with real skill [Fact]. Official macroeconomic regime labels arrive months to years late and are not observable in real time [Fact].

Contested. Whether regimes defined by future direction can be forecast with useful skill from public market data. Most proposed predictors of the equity premium fail out of sample (Welch & Goyal, 2008), and the worked example finds the same for regime labels. Forecasts with sensible restrictions (Campbell & Thompson, 2008) or combinations of many predictors (Rapach, Strauss & Zhou, 2010) recover small but real gains. The disagreement is about whether small means useful; no one finds the large skill a direction regime would need. Whether cross-asset inputs (credit, the curve, the volatility term structure, sentiment) add to price-path inputs for equity regimes. The worked example, which did not test sentiment, finds a gain of at most 0.01 of AUC for its labels; practitioners report gains in credit-led episodes such as 2007, and teacher–student studies report gains for multi-asset allocation. Both sides rest on few episodes. Whether volatility timing improves returns, rather than only risk, out of sample (Moreira & Muir, 2017; Cederburg et al., 2020).

Open. Whether labels defined directly on multi-asset outcomes, such as the stock–bond correlation or a stress event, are forecastable from structure inputs with useful skill. How to share episodes across markets, so that a classifier trained on many countries’ bear markets is less starved of data than one trained on the US alone. And whether the composition changes in option markets since 2020 have created new information in sentiment inputs or destroyed the old.

This chapter’s view, stated as such: a regime study earns its keep as a disciplined measurement of the quantity and price of risk, with probabilities for a few risk-type labels on top. The search for a classifier that tells bull markets from bear markets early is the search for a return forecast, and should be judged as one.

Grouped by kind. Each entry carries one line on why it matters. Practitioner sources name the author’s interest; critiques have their own group. Links go to a free copy where one exists; entries marked paywalled link to the publisher.

10.5 Critiques and cautions

  • Welch, I. & Goyal, A. (2008). “A Comprehensive Look at the Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction.” Review of Financial Studies 21(4), 1455–1508. — Most return predictors fail out of sample: the evidence behind “direction is not learnable”.

10.7 Practitioner sources

Practitioner frameworks are often the clearest statement of how regimes are used, and come from firms that sell products built on them.

  • Podolsky, P., Johnson, R. & Jennings, O. (2012). “The All Weather Story.” Bridgewater Associates. — Four growth–inflation environments and risk balance across them. The firm manages All Weather portfolios.
  • Greetham, T. and colleagues (2004). The Investment Clock. Merrill Lynch. — Reflation, recovery, overheat and stagflation. No public copy located.
  • Faber, M. T. (2007). “A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation.” Journal of Wealth Management 9(4), 69–79. [publisher — paywalled] — The ten-month moving-average rule. The author’s firm runs trend-following funds.

10.8 Data sources

  • Kenneth R. French data library — daily US market and risk-free returns from 1926.
  • Cboe VIX historical data — the VIX and its term-structure and related indices.
  • FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis — BAA10Y, T10Y3M, USREC, NFCI and STLFSI4; ALFRED for vintages.
  • Chicago Fed NFCI — the index, its subindices and documentation.
  • OFR Financial Stress Index — daily, with category and regional contributions.

10.9 If you only read eight things

  1. Ang & Timmermann (2012) — the review of regime models in finance.
  2. Kole & van Dijk (2017) — rules against models for bull and bear markets.
  3. Lunde & Timmermann (2004) — what a turning-point label is and how it behaves.
  4. López de Prado (2018) — labels with reach, and validation that respects it.
  5. Bekaert & Hoerova (2014) — what the VIX contains.
  6. Adrian, Boyarchenko & Giannone (2019) — what financial conditions forecast, and what they do not.
  7. Welch & Goyal (2008) — why direction labels disappoint.
  8. Gneiting & Raftery (2007) — how to score a probability.

Appendix A. Concepts and prerequisites

Everything the main text uses without stopping to explain. Entries are ordered by dependency, not alphabetically, so later entries build on earlier ones. Each gives the idea in words first, then the formal definition, then why it appears here, then where to go deeper. Several entries summarise material that the companion chapter, Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models, develops at length; they link to its appendix rather than repeat it.

A.1 Information sets and look-ahead

The idea. A backtest is honest only if every number it uses was available at the moment the decision was made. The information set \(\mathcal{F}_t\) is the bookkeeping for that: everything published by the close of day \(t\), in the version published then. Look-ahead bias is the use of anything outside it.

Formally. \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\) is a filtration: an increasing family of information sets, \(\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t\) for \(s \le t\). A quantity is \(\mathcal{F}_t\)-measurable if its value is determined by \(\mathcal{F}_t\). In practice the test is operational: could this number have been computed from data published by the close of day \(t\), in the version that existed then? A revised series has a vintage for each publication date, and only the vintage current at \(t\) belongs to \(\mathcal{F}_t\).

Why it appears here. The reach of a label (§1.4) says which information set the label belongs to. The timing table of §3.11 lists when each input enters \(\mathcal{F}_t\), and its rules keep features \(\mathcal{F}_t\)-measurable.

Deeper. Appendix A.1 of Market Regimes and Hidden Markov Models; Williams (1991), chapters 9 and 10; on vintages, Croushore & Stark (2001).

A.2 Conditional probability forecasts

The idea. For a binary label, the best possible forecast is not a guess of 0 or 1 but the probability of 1 given everything known. Every classifier is an attempt to estimate that probability.

Formally. \(p_t = \Pr(y_t = 1 \mid \mathcal{F}_t) = \mathbb{E}[y_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t]\). Among all forecasts built from \(\mathcal{F}_t\) it minimises the expected squared error, and the minimum is \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(y_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t)] = \mathbb{E}[p_t(1 - p_t)]\), because a binary variable with success probability \(p\) has variance \(p(1 - p)\).

Why it appears here. It is the ceiling on any classifier’s accuracy (§1.4), and the reason a label with zero reach needs no model: then \(p_t\) is 0 or 1 and the ceiling is perfection.

Deeper. Williams (1991), chapter 9, on conditional expectation as the best mean-squared-error predictor.

A.3 Persistence and half-life

The idea. A persistent series stays near where it is. Persistence is why yesterday’s regime predicts today’s, why volatility can be forecast, and why daily samples contain far fewer independent observations than days.

Formally. For a first-order autoregression \(x_t = \mu + \rho\,(x_{t-1} - \mu) + e_t\) with \(0 < \rho < 1\), a deviation from the mean shrinks by the factor \(\rho\) each period, so after \(k\) periods it is \(\rho^k\) of its size and it halves after \(\ln 0.5 / \ln \rho\) periods. With \(\rho = 0.98\) per day the half-life is about 34 days. A slope of 0.72 per month gives \(\ln 0.5 / \ln 0.72 \approx 2.1\) months.

Why it appears here. The persistence of volatility makes volatility labels learnable and the stale label a strong baseline (§1.4, §5.1). The lack of persistence in returns makes direction labels flicker (§4.5).

Deeper. Hamilton (1994), chapter 3.

A.4 Sampling error of correlations

The idea. A correlation or autocorrelation estimated from a short window is noisy, and the noise can be as large as the variation the estimate is meant to detect.

Formally. For \(n\) independent pairs with true correlation \(\rho\), the estimate’s standard error is approximately \((1 - \rho^2)/\sqrt{n}\), which is \(1/\sqrt{n}\) at \(\rho = 0\): about 0.13 for \(n = 63\). The approximation needs \(n\) moderately large and the pairs independent; overlapping or persistent data make the error larger. Fisher’s transformation \(\tfrac{1}{2}\ln[(1 + r)/(1 - r)]\) gives an approximately normal statistic with standard error \(1/\sqrt{n - 3}\), which is the better basis for intervals.

Why it appears here. It limits trending-versus-mean-reverting regimes (§2.5) and correlation regimes (§2.9, §3.8).

Deeper. Any mathematical statistics text on the sampling distribution of the correlation coefficient.

A.5 Proper scores and the Brier score

The idea. A scoring rule grades a probability forecast against what happened. It is proper if no forecaster can improve their expected score by reporting anything other than their true belief, which makes scores comparable and honest.

Formally. The Brier score is \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_t (\hat p_t - y_t)^2\) and the log loss \(-\frac{1}{n}\sum_t [y_t \ln \hat p_t + (1 - y_t)\ln(1 - \hat p_t)]\). Both are strictly proper: for an event with true probability \(p\), the expected Brier score of a forecast \(q\) is \(p(1 - q)^2 + (1 - p)q^2\), which is minimised at \(q = p\). Skill against a reference forecast is \(1 - \mathrm{BS}/\mathrm{BS}_{\text{ref}}\). Murphy’s decomposition writes the Brier score as reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty (§7.2).

Why it appears here. Every Brier skill score in §5–§7 is this quantity, with climatology or the stale label as the reference.

Deeper. Gneiting & Raftery (2007); Murphy (1973).

A.6 ROC curves and AUC

The idea. A classifier’s score can be turned into yes-or-no decisions at any threshold. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve shows, for every threshold, the share of positives caught against the share of negatives falsely flagged. The area under it summarises ranking quality in one number.

Formally. With true-positive rate \(\mathrm{TPR}(c) = \Pr(\hat p > c \mid y = 1)\) and false-positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}(c) = \Pr(\hat p > c \mid y = 0)\), the ROC curve plots \(\mathrm{TPR}\) against \(\mathrm{FPR}\) as the threshold \(c\) varies, and \(\mathrm{AUC} = \Pr(\hat p_i > \hat p_j \mid y_i = 1, y_j = 0)\), with ties counted as one half. This is the Mann–Whitney statistic, so the AUC is unchanged by any increasing transformation of the scores. If the scores of positives and negatives are normal with equal variance and means \(d'\) standard deviations apart, \(\mathrm{AUC} = \Phi(d'/\sqrt{2})\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. The precision–recall curve plots \(\Pr(y = 1 \mid \hat p > c)\) against \(\mathrm{TPR}(c)\) and, unlike the ROC curve, depends on the base rate.

Why it appears here. AUC is the ranking score of §1.4, §6.4 and §7.3. It is blind to calibration, which is why the chapter pairs it with the Brier score.

Deeper. Fawcett (2006); Saito & Rehmsmeier (2015).

A.7 Cohen’s kappa

The idea. Two labels can agree on most days simply because both say “calm” most of the time. Kappa corrects for that, measuring agreement beyond what the two base rates would produce by chance.

Formally. With \(p_o\) the observed share of days on which two binary labels agree, and \(p_e = \pi_1 \pi_2 + (1 - \pi_1)(1 - \pi_2)\) the agreement expected if they were independent with base rates \(\pi_1\) and \(\pi_2\), \(\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)\). It is 1 for perfect agreement and 0 for chance-level agreement, and it can be negative. Its maximum attainable value falls when the two base rates differ.

Why it appears here. The agreement table of §6.2 and the stability check of §4.9.

Deeper. Cohen (1960).

A.8 Information coefficient and hit rate

The idea. A forecast of returns is judged by how well it ranks or correlates with what happens. Even a good forecast is right only slightly more often than a coin.

Formally. The information coefficient is the correlation between forecast and outcome. If both are jointly normal with correlation \(\mathrm{IC}\), the probability that they share a sign, the hit rate, is \(\tfrac{1}{2} + \arcsin(\mathrm{IC})/\pi\): 51.6% at an IC of 0.05.

Why it appears here. It calibrates what a direction label can offer (§1.4).

Deeper. Section 2 of Edge as Information.

A.9 Sharpe ratio and drawdown

The idea. The Sharpe ratio measures return per unit of risk; the drawdown measures the worst fall from a peak. One describes the average experience, the other the worst.

Formally. The annualised Sharpe ratio of daily excess returns \(e_t\) is \(\sqrt{A}\,\bar e / s_e\), with \(\bar e\) and \(s_e\) their mean and standard deviation. The drawdown at \(t\) is \(1 - W_t/\max_{s \le t} W_s\) for a wealth path \(W\), and the maximum drawdown is its largest value over the sample.

Why it appears here. The value of the bull–bear label, known in advance or when confirmed, is measured by both (§1.1, §6.3).

Deeper. Section 4 of Edge as Information; Appendix A.25 of the companion chapter, on the Sharpe ratio’s standard error.

A.10 Logistic regression

The idea. Model the log-odds of an event as a weighted sum of inputs. The model produces probabilities between 0 and 1, and its coefficients say how much each input moves the odds.

Formally. \(\Pr(y_t = 1 \mid x_t) = \Lambda(\beta_0 + \beta^\top x_t)\) with \(\Lambda(u) = 1/(1 + e^{-u})\), so \(\ln[p/(1 - p)] = \beta_0 + \beta^\top x_t\). The coefficients maximise the log-likelihood \(\sum_t [y_t \ln \hat p_t + (1 - y_t) \ln(1 - \hat p_t)]\), which is concave, so Newton’s method (iteratively reweighted least squares) finds the unique maximum in a few steps. The probit model replaces \(\Lambda\) with \(\Phi\); the ordered logit applies one coefficient vector to \(K - 1\) cumulative splits of ordered classes; dynamic versions add lagged labels or a lagged index as inputs.

Why it appears here. It is the default classifier of §5.4 and the model of the worked example (§6).

Deeper. Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman (2009), section 4.4.

A.11 Shrinkage

The idea. With few independent observations, estimated coefficients are noisy, and a model that uses them at face value fits noise. Shrinkage pulls the coefficients toward zero, trading a little bias for much less variance.

Formally. Ridge regularisation adds \(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\alpha\, n \lVert \beta \rVert^2\) to the negative log-likelihood of \(n\) rows (§5.4); the lasso uses a multiple of \(\lVert \beta \rVert_1\) instead and sets some coefficients exactly to zero. As the penalty grows the fitted probabilities move toward the base rate. The penalty is chosen by validation or, as in the worked example, fixed in advance.

Why it appears here. In the worked example the twelve-input model lost to a one-input model without shrinkage and matched it with shrinkage (§5.4, §6.4), because the effective sample is a few dozen episodes.

Deeper. Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman (2009), section 3.4; Appendix A.31 of the companion chapter, on shrinkage as partial pooling.

A.12 Calibration

The idea. A score that ranks days well need not be a probability. Calibration maps scores to probabilities that match observed frequencies.

Formally. Platt scaling fits \(\Pr(y = 1 \mid s) = \Lambda(a + b\,s)\) to a score \(s\) by logistic regression; isotonic regression fits the best non-decreasing step function of the score. Both must be fitted on data the scoring model did not train on, out-of-fold or on a later period, because a flexible model’s scores on its own training rows are overconfident.

Why it appears here. Post-processing (§5.11) and the reliability check of §7.2; tree ensembles need it most (§5.5).

Deeper. Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (2005).

A.13 Overlapping labels

The idea. A label defined over the next 63 days shares 62 days of outcome with the label of the following day. A training set of thousands of daily rows then holds far fewer independent pieces of evidence than it appears to.

Formally. For labels over windows of length \(h\), rows at least \(h\) days apart share no outcome days, so \(n\) days contain roughly \(n/h\) non-overlapping labels. When the label is also persistent beyond its window the effective count is lower still, and for a rare regime it approaches the number of episodes. López de Prado’s average uniqueness weights each row by the inverse of the number of labels its window overlaps.

Why it appears here. It is why §4.10 purges, weights and sizes test sets by episodes, and why the worked example’s intervals resample years (§6.1).

Deeper. López de Prado (2018), chapter 4; Appendix A.30 of the companion chapter, on effective sample size.

A.14 Censoring and provisional labels

The idea. At the end of any sample, some labels are not yet decided: the forward window has not elapsed, or the current phase has not ended. Treating the undecided labels as decided is a look-ahead in reverse: it assumes an outcome that has not happened.

Formally. A label with fixed reach \(b\) is censored for the last \(b\) days of the sample. A turning-point label is final up to the current running extreme and provisional after it (§4.10). Survival analysis treats the same problem for durations: a spell still in progress has a known lower bound on its length but no end.

Why it appears here. §4.1, §4.4 and the training rule of §4.10.

Deeper. Any survival-analysis text on right-censoring.

A.15 Purging, embargo and walk-forward validation

The idea. In time-series validation, information leaks from test to training through overlapping labels and through serial dependence. Purging removes the leaking rows; an embargo adds a gap; walk-forward testing only ever predicts the future from the past.

Formally. Walk-forward validation refits at dates \(\tau_1 < \tau_2 < \dots\) on rows before each \(\tau_k\) and tests on \([\tau_k, \tau_{k+1})\). Purging drops any training row whose label window overlaps the test period; an embargo also drops training rows within a fixed gap after it. For a label with reach \(b\), the purge at a refit date \(\tau\) removes training rows with \(t > \tau - b\).

Why it appears here. §4.10 and the worked example’s training rule (“rows whose label was final by the refit date”).

Deeper. López de Prado (2018), chapters 7 and 12; section 11 of the companion chapter and its Appendix A.39.

A.16 Block bootstrap and permutation nulls

The idea. The ordinary bootstrap resamples days independently and so destroys the persistence that makes neighbouring days alike. Resampling blocks of consecutive days keeps it, and gives honest error bars for dependent data. A permutation null asks what score the same pipeline would get if features and labels were unrelated but each kept its own persistence.

Formally. The moving-block bootstrap draws blocks of fixed length with replacement and concatenates them; the stationary bootstrap draws blocks of random, geometrically distributed length (Politis & Romano, 1994). A persistence-preserving permutation shifts the label series circularly against the features by a random offset, refits and records the score; repeated, it gives the score’s distribution under no relationship.

Why it appears here. The 90% intervals of §6.4 resample one-year blocks; §7.6 recommends both tools.

Deeper. Politis & Romano (1994); Appendix A.41 of the companion chapter.

A.17 Multiple testing

The idea. Try enough label definitions, thresholds and inputs and one of them will look good by luck. The best of many trials overstates what any one of them will deliver.

Formally. If \(N\) independent strategies with no edge are tested, the expected best Sharpe ratio grows roughly with \(\sqrt{2 \ln N}\) times its standard error. Corrections either raise the significance threshold with the number of trials or deflate the best result for them.

Why it appears here. §3.1’s warning against testing forty inputs on thirty episodes, and the trial count of §7.6.

Deeper. Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2016); Bailey & López de Prado (2014); Appendix A.40 of the companion chapter.

A.18 Principal components and factor models

The idea. When many inputs move together, a few combinations of them carry most of the variation. Principal components find those combinations; a factor model treats them as unobserved drivers; the Mahalanobis distance measures how unusual a day is once the inputs’ co-movement is taken into account.

Formally. For standardised inputs with correlation matrix \(C\), the principal components are the eigenvectors of \(C\), and the share of total variance explained by the \(k\)-th is its eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues. A dynamic factor model writes each input as loadings times a few latent factors that follow their own time-series process. The squared Mahalanobis distance of a vector \(R\) from mean \(\bar R\) with covariance \(\Sigma\) is \((R - \bar R)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (R - \bar R)\).

Why it appears here. The STLFSI4 is a first principal component and the NFCI comes from a dynamic factor model (§2.7); turbulence is a Mahalanobis distance and the absorption ratio a principal-component share (§2.7, §5.3); §3.13 measures the input space with them.

Deeper. Jolliffe (2002); Appendix A.23 of the companion chapter.

A.19 Clustering

The idea. Clustering groups days whose features look alike, without labels. Each group can then be read as a regime.

Formally. \(k\)-means chooses \(K\) centroids and assigns each day to the nearest, minimising the total squared distance. A Gaussian mixture gives each cluster its own mean and covariance and assigns days probabilistically, fitted by the EM algorithm. Clustering whole return distributions instead of feature vectors needs a distance between distributions, such as the Wasserstein distance (Horvath, Issa & Muguruza, 2024). None of these methods knows that days are ordered in time, so their regimes flicker unless persistence is added (A.26).

Why it appears here. Model-derived labels (§4.6) and the Gaussian-mixture regimes of §2.8.

Deeper. Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman (2009), sections 8.5 and 14.3; Appendix A.22 of the companion chapter.

A.20 Trees and boosting

The idea. A decision tree splits the input space by thresholds and predicts a constant in each region. Many trees combined, by averaging or by adding them in sequence, make a flexible model of interactions and non-linear effects.

Formally. A random forest averages deep trees grown on bootstrap samples with random subsets of inputs (Breiman, 2001). Gradient boosting adds shallow trees one at a time, each fitted to the gradient of the loss at the current prediction (Friedman, 2001). Because each tree predicts a constant beyond the last split, the ensemble cannot extrapolate past the range of its training data.

Why it appears here. §5.5, and the student model of the teacher–student pipelines in §5.8.

Deeper. Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman (2009), chapters 10 and 15; Appendix A.33 of the companion chapter.

A.21 Quantile regression

The idea. Ordinary regression models the average outcome. Quantile regression models a chosen quantile, such as the worst 5% of outcomes, so it can describe how the lower tail moves with conditions even when the average does not.

Formally. The \(q\)-th quantile regression minimises \(\sum_t \rho_q(y_t - x_t^\top \beta)\) with the check loss \(\rho_q(u) = u\,(q - \mathbb{1}[u < 0])\), which weights positive errors by \(q\) and negative errors by \(1 - q\).

Why it appears here. Growth-at-risk (§2.7) and the direct forecast of drawdown risk in §5.10.

Deeper. Koenker & Bassett (1978).

A.22 Hysteresis

The idea. A switch with a single threshold chatters when its input hovers near the threshold. Hysteresis gives it memory: a higher threshold to switch on, a lower one to switch off.

Formally. With entry threshold \(u_{\text{in}}\) above exit threshold \(u_{\text{out}}\), the state turns on when the input reaches \(u_{\text{in}}\), turns off when it falls below \(u_{\text{out}}\), and otherwise stays as it was (§5.2). The gap \(u_{\text{in}} - u_{\text{out}}\) trades delay against the number of switches.

Why it appears here. The real-time ±20% rule is a hysteresis rule (§1.4), and hysteresis is the cheapest cure for flickering regimes (§4.2, §5.11).

Deeper. Section 12 of the companion chapter, on hysteresis bands and trading costs.

A.23 Two-sided filters

The idea. Many smoothing methods estimate the trend at a date from data on both sides of it. They look clean in history but cannot be computed in real time, and their recent values change as new data arrive.

Formally. A two-sided filter computes \(\tilde x_t = \sum_{k=-m}^{m} w_k x_{t+k}\), using \(m\) future values. At the end of a sample it must fall back on a one-sided version, so its last values are revised as data accumulate. The Hodrick–Prescott filter chooses the trend \(\tau_t\) to minimise \(\sum_t (x_t - \tau_t)^2 + \lambda_{\text{HP}} \sum_t (\Delta^2 \tau_t)^2\) over the whole sample, so every fitted value depends on every observation.

Why it appears here. Labels defined by two-sided filters share the look-ahead of turning-point labels (§4.4), and the OECD’s leading indicators use Hodrick–Prescott detrending (§2.8).

Deeper. Hamilton (2018).

A.24 Markov chains and durations

The idea. A Markov chain moves between a few states with fixed probabilities that depend only on the current state. The probability of staying put sets how long states last.

Formally. With transition probabilities \(p_{jk} = \Pr(s_{t+1} = k \mid s_t = j)\), a visit to state \(j\) lasts a geometric number of days with mean \(1/(1 - p_{jj})\): a daily stay probability of 0.98 gives visits averaging 50 days. The stationary distribution gives the long-run share of time in each state.

Why it appears here. The Markov filter that smooths a classifier’s output (§5.11) and the latent-state models of §5.7.

Deeper. Appendices A.4 and A.6 of the companion chapter.

A.25 Hidden Markov models and filtering

The idea. A hidden Markov model treats the regime as an unobserved Markov state and infers it from data. Inference comes in three forms that use different information: predicted (data up to yesterday), filtered (up to today) and smoothed (the whole sample).

Formally. The filter alternates two steps: carry yesterday’s belief through the transition matrix, then reweight each state by how well it explains today’s observation and renormalise (the Hamilton filter). The smoother adds a backward pass that uses later data (the Kim smoother). Dividing a classifier’s probability by its training prior gives a quantity proportional to the likelihood of the observation in each state, which can take the place of the reweighting step (§5.11).

Why it appears here. The dating, nowcasting and forecasting tasks of §1.5 are the smoothed, filtered and predicted beliefs; smoothed probabilities used as labels (§4.6) carry future data.

Deeper. Sections 5 and 6 and Appendices A.10–A.11 of the companion chapter; Bourlard & Morgan (1994) for the hybrid with a classifier.

A.26 Statistical jump models

The idea. A jump model assigns each day to the state whose typical features it is closest to, as clustering does, but charges a fixed penalty for every switch, so states persist.

Formally. It chooses states \(s_1, \dots, s_T\) and centroids \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K\) to minimise \(\sum_t \lVert x_t - \mu_{s_t} \rVert^2 + \lambda \sum_t \mathbb{1}[s_t \ne s_{t-1}]\). Given the centroids, the best state sequence is found exactly by dynamic programming, the same recursion as the Viterbi algorithm for hidden Markov models; given the states, each centroid is the mean of its days. Running the recursion forward only and reading off the best state at each date gives the causal version.

Why it appears here. Model-derived labels (§4.6), teacher–student pipelines (§5.8) and the worked example’s jump-model label (§6).

Deeper. Bemporad et al. (2018); Nystrup, Lindström & Madsen (2020); section 5 of the companion chapter.

A.27 Change-point detection

The idea. Instead of asking which of a few known states the market is in, ask whether its behaviour has just changed.

Formally. A cumulative-sum (CUSUM) detector adds up evidence for a shift, \(C_t = \max(0, C_{t-1} + \ell_t)\) with \(\ell_t\) a log-likelihood ratio of “changed” against “unchanged”, and alarms when \(C_t\) crosses a threshold (Page, 1954). Bayesian online change-point detection keeps a posterior over the run length, the time since the last change, and updates it with each observation (Adams & MacKay, 2007).

Why it appears here. §5.9, as a monitoring layer beside a classifier.

Deeper. Appendix A.21 of the companion chapter.

A.28 Knowledge distillation

The idea. A large or awkward model, the teacher, can train a simpler one, the student, by letting the student imitate the teacher’s outputs. Imitating the teacher’s probabilities passes on more than imitating its hard decisions, because the probabilities carry the teacher’s uncertainty.

Formally. The student minimises a loss against the teacher’s soft targets, for example the cross-entropy \(-\sum_t \sum_k q_t^{(k)} \ln \hat p_t^{(k)}\) with \(q_t^{(k)}\) the teacher’s probability of class \(k\), instead of against one-hot labels.

Why it appears here. Teacher–student regime pipelines (§5.8) are distillation with a two-sided teacher, and soft labels (§4.10) are its targets.

Deeper. Hinton, Vinyals & Dean (2015).

A.29 Realised volatility

The idea. Volatility is not observed directly, but the sum of squared returns over a window estimates it, and the more finely the window is sampled the better the estimate.

Formally. \(\mathrm{RV}^{(n)}_t = \sqrt{(A/n) \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \ell_{t-i}^2}\) annualises the average squared daily log return over \(n\) days. With intraday data, summing squared five-minute returns gives a far more precise daily variance. The heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) model forecasts realised variance from its daily, weekly and monthly averages.

Why it appears here. It is the main price-path input (§3.2), the stale label for volatility targets (§1.4), and the basis of the forward-volatility label (§4.5).

Deeper. Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold & Labys (2003); Corsi (2009); Appendix A.18 of the companion chapter.

A.30 Implied volatility, the VIX and the variance risk premium

The idea. Option prices imply how much volatility buyers expect and how much they will pay for protection against it. The VIX reads that from S&P 500 options for the next 30 days. Because option buyers pay for insurance, implied variance is usually above the variance then realised; the gap is the variance risk premium.

Formally. \(\mathrm{VIX}^2_t/10^4\) approximates the expectation of the annualised variance of the S&P 500 over the next 30 days under risk-neutral probabilities, the probabilities implied by option prices, computed from a strip of out-of-the-money options. The variance risk premium is that expectation minus the expectation under real-world probabilities; a common proxy subtracts trailing realised variance. The VIX term structure compares the same measure over 9 days, 30 days, 3 months and 6 months. It normally slopes upward (contango) and inverts (backwardation) in stress.

Why it appears here. The VIX is the leading forward-looking input (§3.3), and the volatility regimes of §2.3 are bands on it.

Deeper. Sections 5 and 6 of Implied Volatility; the Cboe VIX methodology; Bekaert & Hoerova (2014).

A.31 Credit spreads and the excess bond premium

The idea. A corporate bond yields more than a government bond of similar maturity because it might default, because investors demand a premium for bearing that risk, and because it is harder to trade. The extra yield, the spread, rises with all three.

Formally. A yield spread subtracts a government yield from a corporate yield; the Baa–10-year spread uses Moody’s Baa index and the 10-year Treasury. An option-adjusted spread is the constant spread over the government curve that prices a bond after removing the value of options embedded in it, such as the issuer’s right to call it. The excess bond premium is the part of corporate spreads left after accounting for each firm’s expected default, so it isolates the price of risk.

Why it appears here. Credit is the price-of-risk input of §3.4 and the second factor of §3.13.

Deeper. Sections 8 and 9 of Bonds and Bond Markets; Gilchrist & Zakrajšek (2012).

A.32 The term spread

The idea. Long-term interest rates embed expected future short rates. When markets expect the central bank to cut, typically because they expect a slowdown, long rates fall below short rates and the curve inverts.

Formally. The term spread is a long yield minus a short yield, for example the 10-year minus 3-month Treasury yield. The near-term forward spread compares the forward rate implied for six quarters ahead with the current short rate. Both also contain a term premium, the extra return demanded for holding long bonds, which varies over time.

Why it appears here. It is the classic recession predictor (§2.8, §3.5) and the slow second factor of §3.13.

Deeper. Section 11 of Bonds and Bond Markets; Estrella & Mishkin (1998).

A.33 Stress and conditions indices

The idea. Financial stress shows up at once in many places: spreads widen, volatility rises, funding markets strain. A stress index averages many such measurements so that the common movement stands out from the noise of each.

Formally. Each input is standardised against its history, and the index is a weighted sum, \(I_t = \sum_j w_j \tilde x_{j,t}\), with weights from a first principal component, a dynamic factor model, or a correlation-based scheme (§5.3). Indices are usually scaled so that zero is the historical average.

Why it appears here. §2.7 uses them as regimes and §3.6 as inputs; their revisions and full-sample weights are the main hazards.

Deeper. Kliesen & Smith (2010); Brave & Butters (2012); Hollo, Kremer & Lo Duca (2012); Monin (2019).

A.34 Survivorship bias

The idea. A data set that contains only the survivors, such as today’s index members or funds still in business, describes a past better than the one that happened, because the losers have been removed.

Formally. If membership at the end of the sample depends on performance during it, any statistic computed over today’s members is conditioned on an outcome that was not known at the time, which is a form of look-ahead.

Why it appears here. Breadth and correlation inputs built from current index members (§3.7, §3.8).

Deeper. Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross (1992).

A.35 Variance ratio and Hurst exponent

The idea. If returns are independent, the variance of \(q\)-day returns is \(q\) times the variance of one-day returns. Departures from that scaling reveal trending or mean reversion.

Formally. \(\mathrm{VR}(q) = \operatorname{Var}(r_{t-q+1} + \dots + r_t) / [q \operatorname{Var}(r_t)]\), which equals \(1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{q-1}(1 - k/q)\rho_k\) in terms of the return autocorrelations \(\rho_k\): above one when they are positive (trending), below one when negative (mean reverting). The Hurst exponent \(H\) describes the same scaling as a power law, with the range of cumulative deviations growing like \(n^H\); \(H = \tfrac{1}{2}\) for independent returns.

Why it appears here. The trending-versus-mean-reverting regimes of §2.5.

Deeper. Lo & MacKinlay (1988).
